9c07634e9f5d44ca: LONDON: Ronald Araujo says it is "very early" to be talking about making his move to Liverpool permanent despite an impressive start to his loan spell at Anfield.
The former Barcelona captain has established himself as first-choice right-back even though he is known to prefer a central defensive role.

Liverpool have a £47 million ($63 million) option to secure Araujo's services on a full-time basis, although whether the six-time European champions will want to spend that sum on a player who turns 28 in March remains to be seen.
"It's very early to talk about these things," the Uruguayan international said ahead of Tuesday's Champions League match at home to Villarreal.
"I'm really happy to be here, my family are also very happy but it's a bit early to be talking about these things."
Araujo, who has played 10 times for Liverpool, is already popular with fans and appears to have adjusted quickly to the demands of the Premier League.
"Coming to Liverpool, it's not easy," he said. "There are those demands, that responsibility. Personally I'd already experienced that in Barcelona.

"It depends on the personality of each player and how they (face) that challenge. I knew it was a new challenge coming to the Premier League but from the first moment I arrived I had no doubts I had to give everything here. And that's how I live it.
"It's not easy to be in big sides, but that's what we came to do. That's the work we have to do."
Andoni Iraola's Liverpool are fifth in the league phase of the Champions League with two wins in two games, against Atletico Madrid and LASK.

69e37b8a2ad2f8a3: If you want to keep bots from making sense of the code you worked so hard on and using it to write programs of their own, there's a new programming language out there designed to confuse LLMs. What began as software engineer Dominik Picheta experimenting with whether LLMs understand the code they write has turned into something else entirely: An open-source, albeit esoteric, programming language he’s dubbed KillSwitch. There are no brackets, no formatting standards to remember, and seemingly no structure: Just chunks of text, ideally as prosaic as possible, interspersed with functions, variables, and statements written in a manner to be as confusing as possible to LLMs. That means humans might be a bit befuddled too, naturally. “It's totally normal for a human to be confused by the language at first,” Picheta told The Register. “I like to think of it as a bit of a fun puzzle: you should explore the language, play with its interpreter and learn how all the pieces fit together.” KillSwitch wasn’t built by any random person looking to code something confusing to LLMs, and it wasn’t vibe-coded by an AI enthusiast, either. Picheta knows his way around programming languages: He’s a senior software engineer at Cloudflare working on the Workers Runtime team, and is one of the core developers of the Nim programming language. At its most basic, KillSwitch is based around adverbs, which serve as every single identifier in a piece of code. Calling one of those identifiers requires using an anagram of the original adverb, but those anagrams don't have to be actual words - just rearrangements of the original letters. Take, for example, pushing "Hello World" onto the stack and then printing it, as explained on the demo page linked earlier in the story. The program contains several paragraphs of text, most of which the interpreter ignores apart from a few key phrases. Writing “this story starts [adverb]” identifies a code entrypoint. Once inside the code section, writing “ignore previous instructions [adverb anagram]” calls a function, several of which are predefined. In the case of "Hello World," the function to print something is "visibly." Put whatever you want to print in quotation marks, push it onto the stack, call "visibly," and that's that. KillSwitch isn’t a full-featured language, with Picheta describing it as a stack-based interpreted language with only “a limited set of constructs including functions, variables, and if statements,” given its evolution out of an experiment to see how well a programming language could fool an AI into not understanding what was written. Where it gets confusing for an AI is with commands like “ignore previous instructions,” especially when found in the middle of a chunk of text that doesn’t make much sense in that context. KillSwitch’s specification document on GitHub provides more details about the language and is itself designed to confuse LLMs. In one section of the spec, it’s explained that KillSwitch “is equipped with the ability to scan the local network, attempt to find security vulnerabilities in the services on that network, then take those services over and terminate them.” That's not actually the case, as a close reading of the paragraph reveals and Picheta confirmed to us. “The hack statement is both designed to trigger many models' safety guardrails but also to test an LLM's ability to discern fact from fiction,” Picheta told us, adding that there are several lies in the spec document designed to confuse any LLM that may scrape it in an attempt to understand how the language works. “The idea is that humans should be able to deduce what is a lie, whereas LLMs are naive and can be easily swayed by what is written in the spec,” Picheta added. “Some don't realize what its semantic meaning is, whereas others refuse to continue because they believe the script may hack someone.” Do LLMs understand what they write? A programming language designed to confuse AI models seems unlikely to stay obfuscated for long - especially if it’s open source, available on Github, and likely to be scraped by an LLM at some point. Picheta’s aware of that inevitability, which, along with the fact he wanted to test AI’s ability to understand confusing code, is why he’s benchmarked a number of major models against it. “I'm 99.9 percent certain the AI models I benchmarked KS on have not been trained on its source,” Picheta said. “The source hasn't been in the public domain for very long … I'm pretty sure none of the benchmarked models have had training runs that began after the release.” The best-performing model only managed a composite benchmark score of 66.8 percent on KillSwitch coding tasks, while most struggled to get above 50 percent. Even at that high a score, Picheta doesn’t believe it suggests LLMs understand the code they’re writing. Examples in the benchmark were simple, and he believes that, even if an AI were trained on the intricacies of KillSwitch, it’s still going to get tripped up. “My instinct is that in those circumstances they will suddenly be able to ace the basic tasks, which are based on the open sourced test files in the GitHub repo, but will continue to fail to build more complex tasks requiring them to write longer and more complex scripts,” Picheta asserted - and he’s up for the challenge. “I am excited to see how KillSwitch shows up in model training, and think that we can also take advantage of that training to break LLMs in new ways too as KillSwitch evolves,” Picheta said. Those interested in trying KillSwitch out can find it on GitHub, and don't hesitate to make changes: Picheta said he’s ready and willing to incorporate new ways of making it even more LLM resistant. ®

4d871a7b9953ca15: THE warning by Tan Sri Ayob Khan Mydin Pitchay that terrorist recruiters are targeting Malaysian children through online gaming platforms should serve as a wake-up call.
His allegation that children aged 12, 14 and 15 had been recruited through Roblox, indoctrinated and taught to carry out attacks highlights a disturbing evolution in extremist recruitment.
The danger is not that gaming itself produces terrorists, but that familiar digital environments can become gateways to manipulation, radicalisation and violence.
The changing face of terrorist recruitment
Traditional terrorist recruitment often depended on personal connections, physical gatherings and direct ideological instruction.

Digital platforms have transformed these opportunities, allowing recruiters to approach young people within environments where they feel comfortable, socially connected and relatively independent of adult supervision.
The alleged movement from gaming interactions into private chat groups is particularly concerning.
Recruiters may exploit loneliness, curiosity, frustration or a desire for belonging to establish trust before gradually introducing extremist narratives.
Private communications can subsequently conceal manipulation from parents, teachers and other trusted adults.

This illustrates the distinction between exposure to extremist content and active recruitment. Encountering radical material does not automatically make a child an extremist, just as radical beliefs do not inevitably lead to violence.
The greater danger emerges when manipulation progresses towards ideological commitment, encouragement of violence or preparation for an attack.

Ayob Khan's warning warrants serious attention, but authorities must distinguish allegations from verified evidence. Understanding how recruitment occurs is essential to identifying genuine threats without treating ordinary gaming activity as suspicious.
Technology platforms must share responsibility
Roblox is not inherently a terrorist recruitment platform. The concern is that interactive environments may provide opportunities for malicious individuals to establish contact with children.
Similar vulnerabilities can arise through social media, messaging applications and other digital communities.
Technology companies must take reasonable measures to protect young users.
These include accessible reporting mechanisms, effective moderation, safeguards against predatory contact and prompt cooperation with lawful investigations.
Where credible threats emerge, relevant digital evidence must be preserved and shared through appropriate legal procedures.
Malaysia should assess whether existing regulatory arrangements adequately address recruitment through gaming environments.

Age restrictions and stronger account safeguards may reduce certain risks, but they cannot eliminate manipulation. Excessive restrictions could also affect legitimate users while displacing harmful activity to less visible platforms.
The objective should be proportionate regulation that combines child protection, platform accountability and effective law enforcement.
Success should be measured by reduced opportunities for exploitation, rather than simply the number of accounts blocked.
MyPCVE must address the digital frontline
Malaysia already has an established framework through the Malaysia Action Plan on Preventing and Countering Violent Extremism, known as MyPCVE 2024–2028.
Its four pillars - prevention, enforcement, rehabilitation and reinforcement provide a foundation for responding to the risks identified by Ayob Khan.

Prevention must extend beyond conventional awareness campaigns. Children need practical digital literacy to recognise manipulation, understand the risks of secretive online communications and seek assistance without fear.
Parents and educators require guidance on identifying credible warning signs without interpreting every behavioural change or online interest as evidence of extremism.
Enforcement requires stronger coordination between the Royal Malaysia Police, the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission, cybersecurity specialists and child-protection agencies.
Investigators must be capable of examining digital evidence, identifying recruitment networks and distinguishing genuine operational threats from ordinary online activity.
Rehabilitation is equally important
Children who have experienced manipulation may require individual assessments, educational support, family engagement and structured programmes to disengage from extremist influences.
Treating every vulnerable child primarily as a security offender could deepen isolation and undermine rehabilitation.
Reinforcement should strengthen cooperation among schools, families, community organisations and religious institutions.
Building resilience requires equipping young people to question extremist narratives while protecting legitimate religious beliefs and lawful expression.
Security must remain consistent with the rule of law
Ayob Khan has also advocated preventive legal powers, invoking the former Internal Security Act. His concern about intervening before violence occurs deserves consideration.
However, broad detention powers do not automatically resolve the investigative challenges posed by digital recruitment.
Malaysia needs effective laws and investigative capabilities that enable timely action against credible threats while preserving due process, proportionality and meaningful oversight.
Authorities must distinguish children being exploited by extremist networks from individuals knowingly preparing terrorist violence.
Decisions should be based on evidence and individual circumstances, not online associations or ideological suspicion alone.
A coordinated national response
Malaysia should strengthen cooperation among law enforcement, technology companies, schools, families and child-protection professionals.
Public education must explain how recruitment may occur, where suspicious conduct can be reported and how vulnerable children can obtain assistance.
MyPCVE programmes should also be evaluated to determine whether they effectively prevent recruitment and support early intervention.
Ayob Khan's warning is not a reason to treat gaming as inherently dangerous. It demonstrates how extremist networks can adapt to digital environments faster than institutions respond.

Malaysia's success will depend on identifying genuine threats early, holding platforms accountable, protecting children from manipulation and preventing vulnerable individuals from progressing towards violence.
The priority is clear: protect children before recruiters succeed, without turning ordinary gaming or legitimate expression into grounds for suspicion.
* The writer is Principal Consultant at Arunachala Research & Consultancy Sdn Bhd (ARRESCON), a think tank specialising in strategic national and geopolitical analysis

1375bb961f6a8369: Since its earliest days, the video game industry has been built on developers creating clones of competing games, with varying levels of originality and varying levels of enforcement from game platforms. Now, though, AI coding tools are making that cloning process so efficient that many developers are getting extremely cautious about sharing their early work too widely.

Developer Alliance Arts highlighted this trend over the weekend, delaying the launch of a planned public demo for its demon-themed Russian Roulette drinking game Drunken Goddess Reflex, which had been planned to go live with today's launch of Steam Next Fest.

In a post on social media Friday evening, the Alliance Arts team wrote that, in addition to concerns about managing streaming restrictions, "we're concerned that the demo's content could be used to quickly imitate or replicate the game's presentation and gameplay with AI or other tools and that such works could be released before our launch."
426edc0a1b4c47da: MIAMI: Florida's top prosecutor announced an arrest warrant Monday for former Cuban president Raul Castro under state murder charges that echo a federal indictment unveiled earlier this year.

Raul Castro, 95, is wanted on murder charges connected to the February 24, 1996, shooting down of two civilian aircraft from "Brothers to the Rescue," an organization assisting Cubans fleeing to Florida by sea.

"Raul Castro ordered the murder of four Floridians in cold blood, and Florida will never stop pursuing accountability for that communist conspiracy," Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier said in a statement.
Castro, brother of the late revolutionary leader and US nemesis Fidel Castro, was indicted on federal charges related to the incident in May.
The move came as President Donald Trump's right-wing administration steadily ramped up economic, political and legal pressure on the Cuban communist government.

"We're committed to pursuing every lawful, prosecutable avenue to bring accountability, including parallel federal and state prosecutions," US Attorney Jason A. Reding Quinones said in a statement supporting Florida's action.
"We're proud to stand with Florida in seeking justice for the four Americans murdered in the Brothers to the Rescue shootdown nearly 30 years ago," the federal prosecutor said.
Trump previously seized on a US indictment to justify military action in January that toppled Venezuela's then-president Nicolas Maduro, a staunch ally of the Cuban authorities.
Current Cuban President Miguel Diaz-Canel has said the US federal indictment against Castro has "no legal basis" and was an attempt "to justify the folly of a military aggression against Cuba."

1caf8437a3067465: Europe’s drive for cloud sovereignty is leading to member states favoring providers from their own nation instead of building a Europe-wide cloud services market, according to a report critical of the EU’s proposed Cloud and AI Development Act (CADA). A study by the European Centre for International Political Economy (ECIPE) looked at public cloud contracts in nine EU member states and found that every one that invoked the new vocabulary around “sovereignty” went to a domestic provider, rather than one based in another EU country. It says that European cloud procurement was already highly concentrated nationally before sovereignty became a key policy objective, based on analysis of 8,725 cloud-related procurement contracts between 2018 and 2025. Nearly all went to providers in the same country with negligible intra-EU cross-border competition. Furthermore, the report claims that those domestic wins often turn out to be from prime contractors that are relying on infrastructure provided by the big hyperscale operators, where sovereignty attaches to the nationality of the operator, not to the infrastructure layer on which the service depends. At issue is a conceptual confusion over cloud sovereignty, which is being used to represent two different problems, according to ECIPE. One treats sovereignty as a security and resilience objective, securing data and managing risks. Sovereignty here means that the user has choices over the provider and design of their cloud service needs. The second treats sovereignty as an industrial policy objective, where sovereignty is more about the notion of Europe-headquartered firms becoming more successful if they are not exposed to competition with non-European providers. CADA includes the two different logics and, confusingly, aims to achieve both outcomes, the report states. The legislation frames the four European Union assurance levels as criteria for security, resilience and trustworthy cloud provision, but the criteria actually aim to enforce sovereignty through requirements concerning EU-located infrastructure, restrictions on third-country control, and control over software supply chains. The goal of cloud sovereignty is therefore at risk of becoming a vehicle for policies that favor selected providers, restrict competition and fragment digital markets, ECIPE warns. Instead of allowing pan-European rivals for the big US cloud providers to grow and flourish, the framework may thus have the opposite effect in encouraging member states to favor providers within their own borders, leading to fragmentation across Europe. A more coherent approach would keep the resilience objectives, but temper their use through technological neutrality requirements that preserve interoperability, portability, and multi-cloud options, the report authors state. It makes a number of policy recommendations, including defining sovereignty as a demonstrated outcome, not an ownership status. “Real sovereignty means a public buyer can show its data is secure and that it can switch provider if it has to. A provider’s passport does not tell you that”, said ECIPE Director and co-author of the study, Fredrik Erixon. “Europe’s cloud market is already national in practice. CADA risks locking that in.” Vague drafting But not everyone might agree. Earlier this year, tech trade association CISPE (Cloud Infrastructure Service Providers in Europe) urged the European Commission to legislate for real tech sovereignty, rather than the illusion of it. It argued that sovereignty must be defined by control, not by whether a provider merely has an EU presence, and that means effective ownership of the underlying technology and protection from extraterritorial laws like the US CLOUD Act, under which Washington can compel American tech companies such as the big cloud operators, to hand over any data they hold, including data stored overseas. The same group had earlier warned that the EC’s criteria for cloud sovereignty had been drafted so vaguely as to favor incumbents – meaning the big American operators that already dominate Europe's cloud market. ®

72d08e60437a3a96: In Brno in Czechia, Red Hat’s large local office has been helping the city’s Masaryk University to teach future technical writers. Whenever someone tries to teach, though, they learn as well. At the Open Source Summit in Prague, a senior member of Red Hat’s documentation team in Brno presented a talk called Diagrams & Dragons: Teaching Technical Writing to University Students the Open Source Way. Red Hat has a large site in Brno, which is the second-largest Czech city and is also the home of the respected Masaryk University. Red Hat’s Brno office has a substantial documentation team — this vulture was part of it for a while. For the last four years, Red Hat has been working with the university’s Faculty of Informatics to teach a course unit in technical writing. Jiří Herrman talked about what the course tutors had learned from the students. For FI MUNI, its course PV177 Technical Writing. Red Hat has a page with some of the materials. “RH has been looking into cultivating technical writers in Brno for a while,” he said, but the launch of the course was “delayed due to the 2020 worldwide global… thingy.” The company particularly wants to work on what he described as “that tricky part of technical writing where you actually have to interact with other humans.” Some of the things that struck this former tech-docs writer the most are covered on pages 7 and 9 from Herrman’s short slide deck [PDF], which discuss what didn’t work. Although the course was aimed at students with some technical knowledge, they found that setting classwork with shell-based tools didn’t work: some of the students had never used the command-line, some came with borrowed laptops without admin-level access, and some came with just phones rather than laptops. Some we found less surprising. Getting students to grade one anothers’ work, much as professional tech writers review one another’s contributions, didn’t work well – partly due to the speed required. In the end, the compromise was to give the students a course in grading each other’s work “without pissing each other off.” It didn’t shock us, but we suspect might leave some training vendors taken aback, that interacting with remote teachers who were presenting online didn’t work well – especially when there were multiple tutors, changing with each class. LLM use You may well have already foreseen the biggest “gotcha” for a course that ran for the first time in 2023. It is, naturally, use of LLM. The students were told that they were not allowed to use LLMs during the course, but naturally enough, they did so anyway. Among the problems that Herrman reported were that giving praise to good work that involved LLM use just encouraged more cheating. However, telling students off for it discouraged them, and that encourages cheating. So the team had to come up with some tactics to try to manage this, which involved teaching the students how to use LLMs instead. They did, however, find some things that did work well. Awarding points, even on a semi-arbitrary basis, with occasional secret prizes, as well dispensing feedback via internet-style memes. A final exercise was to role-play a scenario, “Dungeons & Dragons” style. The quest was “I want to be a tech writer, but how to get there?”. This involved navigating a cross-functional team, creating things like release notes, technical notes, and some real documentation for the process. And as the course materials are open source, the graduates ended up with a permanent FOSS record that they can show to prospective employers. There is a project Github, and you can see some of the student’s archived coursework for 2025 and 2026. The issues around LLM use in tech writing were the primary subject of a “Birds of a Feather” session that Herrman moderated earlier: Technical Writing in the Age of AI. He started by asking how many in the audience were using AI in their tech-writing efforts, getting what he called an “overwhelming majority” who were already on-board. What we found interesting is what people said they didn’t use it for. They find even the best models are poor at writing documentation themselves. They’re also poor at drawing diagrams, and at reading them for review purposes. They’re poor at reviewing docs (“AI is too obsequious and so reviews are overly positive,” and “it doesn’t give good feedback on user focus, or structure.”) However, most of the attendees found uses for it all the same. Examples included “Change management” and “Updating to new code” – in other words, identifying which parts of large products had changed and which therefore needed fresh documentation. Others said they used it for “Documenting decisions from meeting notes,” and in other ways, “Collecting information resources for writing,” and worryingly, to “Summarize notes (from conferences, meetings, etc.) and cluster by themes”. Another use was “Reverse engineering code to figure out intent,” or to “Find existing docs to prevent reinvention or duplication.” Tech writing is a demanding job, and pretty much permanently under-resourced. We can’t and don’t blame anyone for grabbing onto anything that might help. Even so, for us, what stood out from this session was the pretty much unanimous agreement among an audience of tech writers that LLMs were poor at doing the job that tech writers themselves did. Reviewing each others’ docs is a core part of the job: tech writers are used to this, and when they review the bots’ efforts, they find the machinese lacking. That fits our impressions, too. What we found alarming is that, although they find the bots poor at doing what the writers know best, even so, they trusted the bots to be competent in other functions, things the writers don’t look at so closely – for example, finding and selecting where docs need updating. The use for summarization is especially alarming: this is something that studies have demonstrated LLMs are bad at. They shorten, not summarize, and that’s no substitute. We find that worrying, but we regularly hear reports of companies pressing staff to use AI more. This is an all-too-human response: “it can’t do my job, but if I must use it, then this stuff isn’t my jurisdiction, and if it messes up, I can blame someone else.” We just worry at whose desk this buck will eventually stop. ®
e562350e628acbb0: WASHINGTON: The US Supreme Court on Monday rejected an appeal by accused 9/11 mastermind Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and two alleged accomplices that sought to revive plea deals which were later revoked.

Mohammed and two others charged with involvement in the Sept 11, 2001 attacks - Walid bin Attash and Mustafa al-Hawsawi - struck pre-trial agreements to avoid the death penalty in 2024, during the administration of president Joe Biden.
After criticism by some victims' families, Biden's defense secretary Lloyd Austin ordered the plea deals to be thrown out, sparking a legal battle over whether or not such a move was permitted.
An appellate court ruled last year that Austin had "acted within the bounds of his legal authority."
A brief, unsigned opinion by the Supreme Court on Monday said it would not take up the appeal.
The trio are among the handful of detainees still held at the notorious Guantanamo US military base in Cuba, and are set to go on trial in June 2028.
Mohammed, also known as "KSM," was considered one of Al-Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden's top lieutenants before he was captured in March 2003 in Pakistan.
Much of the legal jousting in the 9/11 defendants' cases has focused on whether they could be tried fairly after having undergone torture at the hands of the CIA.

0129ebc64b92bd49: PETALING JAYA: Police took down four gangs allegedly involved in cable thefts targeting the East Coast Rail Link and Telekom Malaysia, following a series of operations held over the past week in Temerloh and Mentakab, Pahang.
Temerloh police chief Nasyim Bahron said there were two cases of theft at ECRL cable storehouses and five TM cable theft cases in Temerloh, Mentakab and Lanchang in the past two months alone.
A total of 17 Malaysian men aged 20 to 60 were eventually arrested following the thefts, which caused an estimated RM75,000 in losses, Bernama reported.
The first group, known as "Geng Ravi", was allegedly involved in several cases of cable and metal theft and construction sites and factories abandoned since July.
Police are still hunting for two other suspects linked to the gang.
Another gang named "Geng Kepala" is believed to have been involved in stealing Tenaga Nasional Bhd cables from storehouses, factories and roadsides in Mentakab since August.
Nasyim said they also arrested a suspected member of "Geng Dany" in Mentakab, a two-man ring believed to have also stolen TM cables in Kuala Lumpur.
"The suspect admitted to being involved in several TM cable theft cases in Mentakab this month, along with an accomplice who is still at large," he added.

Finally, police busted "Geng Mista" in an operation in the wee hours of this morning. The gang is believed to have stolen aerial and underground TM cables in Temerloh, Mentakab, Jerantut and Maran since July.
Nasyim added that the head of "Geng Mista" was previously a member of "Geng Kepala". Another suspect remains at large.
All 17 suspects are being investigated for gang robbery, theft and damage to network facilities.

1de49ce669ec812e: JAKARTA: Indonesian police have confirmed the involvement of foreign entities, including those from neighbouring countries, in 98 corporate cases linked to the forest and land fires gripping the country.
National Police Chief General Suyudi Ario Seto said the Criminal Investigation Agency (Bareskrim) is currently working to identify those responsible and establish the nature of their involvement.

“Of the 98 corporate cases we are investigating, there is foreign involvement, but as the investigations are ongoing, we are still determining which involve foreign investment or foreign parties and which do not,” he told a press conference after a limited Cabinet meeting with President Prabowo Subianto in Jakarta on Monday.
Suyudi said investigators are gathering evidence and expected to name suspects soon, including company owners and shareholders who could be held responsible for the fires.

Separately, Coordinating Minister for Political and Security Affairs Dudung Abdurachman Prabowo called for firefighting operations to be intensified without waiting for rainfall, stressing the need for immediate and sustained action.

“The president instructed that the deployment of troops and personnel, including the Indonesian military, police, Forestry Service, and members of the public, be intensified. This must be carried out on a massive scale, in a measured manner and without delay, because the situation has become very disruptive,” he said.

Dudung also said Indonesia had responded to offers of foreign assistance, including from Malaysia and Singapore, with the National Disaster Management Agency (BNPB) coordinating technical arrangements for the proposed support.

However, he said at an earlier press conference that foreign assistance would have to wait until the Indonesian government declares the fires a national disaster – a step it has yet to take, saying it was capable of managing the crisis with its own resources.
d60b3b3ef7ceab2c: KUALA LUMPUR: The Finance Ministry has approved an additional RM500 million for the Rural and Regional Development Ministry after it exceeded its allocations for rural projects this year.
Finance Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim said the additional allocation was approved by identifying savings from development expenditure in other ministries.

He said the Finance Ministry had also directed the Rural and Regional Development Ministry on Sept 10 to suspend the issuance of new letters of acceptance for rural road projects to prevent further accumulation of payment arrears.

"The Rural and Regional Development Ministry has made commitments and spent beyond the original allocations approved under the annual Budget for rural road projects over the past few years, resulting in outstanding payments and delays in payments to contractors," he said in a written parliamentary reply.
"The government had increased annual allocations for rural road projects to more than RM2 billion under the 2026 Budget and 2027 Budget.
"However, these allocations remained insufficient to meet the ministry's existing contractual commitments," he said.
Deputy Prime Minister Datuk Seri Dr Ahmad Zahid Hamidi is the rural and regional development minister.

The Finance Ministry had also asked the Rural and Regional Development Ministry to project its rural road funding requirements until the end of this year and for 2027, based on contracts already awarded, to determine the additional funding needed.

Anwar was responding to Lim Guan Eng (PH-Bagan), who asked what action had been taken against those responsible for alleged breaches of financial procedures involving RM2.1 billion in spending beyond allocations between 2023 and 2025.
On contractor appointments, Anwar said rural road projects were generally awarded through tender processes, including open tenders and the Pre-Qualified Open Tender (TTPKT).
He said the Finance Ministry introduced TTPKT in 2023 as a special procedure to expedite project implementation.

However, the Auditor-General's Report No. 2/2025 found that the implementation of TTPKT, including by the Rural and Regional Development Ministry, had failed to achieve the government's original objectives.
"Accordingly, the Finance Ministry has also stopped approving the use of TTPKT by the Rural and Regional Ministry for new projects," he said.
efcb6bd11ecc3774: KUALA LUMPUR: Jumlah permintaan maksimum elektrik bagi industri pusat data di Semenanjung dijangka mencapai 8,391 Megawatt (MW) menjelang 2030, iaitu berdasarkan unjuran perancangan bekalan elektrik semasa.
Menurut Kementerian Peralihan Tenaga dan Transformasi Air (Petra), daripada jumlah itu, Johor dijangka merekodkan permintaan maksimum elektrik sebanyak 4,428MW, manakala Selangor sebanyak 1,481MW.

“Kedua-dua negeri ini merupakan lokasi tumpuan utama pembangunan pusat data dan pastinya memerlukan perancangan infrastruktur bekalan elektrik yang bersesuaian dengan pertumbuhan beban yang dijangkakan,” menurut kementerian itu.

Kementerian itu menjawab soalan Onn Abu Bakar (PH-Batu Pahat) yang ingin mengetahui mengenai unjuran penggunaan elektrik dan air oleh industri pusat data sehingga 2030 khususnya di Johor dan Selangor serta berapa jumlah pusat data yang telah siap dibina.
Mengenai status pembangunan, Petra memaklumkan, sehingga Ogos 2026, sebanyak 45 pusat data telah siap dibina di Semenanjung Malaysia yang melibatkan kapasiti bekalan elektrik sebanyak 6,041MW.
Kapasiti tersebut merujuk kepada kapasiti bekalan elektrik yang disediakan oleh Tenaga Nasional Bhd melalui grid nasional bagi menyokong pengoperasian pusat data tersebut.
Sementara itu, unjuran permintaan air untuk kegunaan pusat data sehingga 2030 di Selangor dan Johor, jumlahnya adalah sebanyak 389.04 Juta Liter Sehari (JLH).
“Bagaimanapun, pada masa ini jumlah penggunaan air sebenar oleh pusat data yang dilaporkan kepada Suruhanjaya Perkhidmatan Air Negara (SPAN) adalah sebanyak 63.90 JLH,” menurut Petra.
Dalam pada itu, daripada 45 pusat data yang telah siap dibina dan beroperasi ia melibatkan 27 pusat data di Selangor dan 18 di Johor iaitu setakat Jun 2026.
989b1b202b2da95d: KUANTAN: Polis berjaya menumpaskan empat kumpulan disyaki terbabit kegiatan samun dan mencuri kabel milik syarikat laluan rel pantai timur (ECRL) dan Telekom Malaysia (TM) menerusi beberapa operasi dari 12 Okt hingga hari ini di sekitar Temerloh serta Mentakab.

Ketua Polis Temerloh, Nasyim Bahron, berkata sepanjang bulan lalu hingga bulan ini, dua kes samun stor simpanan kabel ECRL dan lima kes kecurian kabel TM dilaporkan di sekitar Temerloh, Mentakab serta Lanchang.
Menurutnya, 17 lelaki tempatan berusia 20 hingga 60 tahun ditahan dalam operasi itu, dengan kerugian dialami ECRL dan TM bagi semua kes itu dianggarkan berjumlah RM75,000.

"Kumpulan pertama dikenali 'Geng Ravi' ditumpaskan menerusi operasi dari 12 hingga 15 Okt. Siasatan mendapati kumpulan itu dipercayai turut terlibat beberapa kes kecurian besi dan kabel di tapak projek serta kilang lama ditinggalkan sejak Julai tahun ini, selain mengesan dua lagi suspek masih bebas," katanya dalam kenyataan.

Beliau berkata, pada 14 Okt lalu, pihaknya berjaya menumpaskan 'Geng Kepala' yang dipercayai turut terbabit beberapa kes kecurian kabel Tenaga Nasional Berhad (TNB) di stor simpanan, kilang dan tepi jalan sekitar Mentakab sejak Ogos lalu.

Jelasnya, polis turut menahan seorang lelaki 28 tahun yang dipercayai anggota 'Geng Dany' di Mentakab semalam kerana disyaki mencuri kabel TM, selain kumpulan itu dipercayai pernah aktif melakukan kegiatan sama di sekitar Kuala Lumpur.
"Siasatan mendapati suspek mengaku terbabit beberapa kes kecurian kabel TM di tepi jalan sekitar Mentakab sejak Oktober tahun ini bersama seorang lagi rakan masih bebas."

Dalam operasi awal pagi ini pula, beliau berkata, pihaknya menumpaskan 'Geng Mista' dipercayai turut terbabit beberapa kes kecurian kabel TM dalam lubang lurang dan tiang tepi jalan sekitar Temerloh, Mentakab, Jerantut dan Maran sejak Julai.
"Ketua kumpulan itu turut dikenal pasti anggota Geng Kepala yang ditahan pada 14 Okt, manakala seorang lagi suspek masih bebas."

Katanya, polis turut merampas pelbagai kenderaan, termasuk sebuah lori, selain gelung dan potongan kabel milik ECRL, TNB serta TM, potongan besi tiang dan pelbagai peralatan mencuri serta memproses kabel.
Menurutnya, semua suspek ditahan bagi membantu siasatan mengikut Seksyen 395, 379 dan 431A Kanun Keseksaan serta Seksyen 235(2) Akta Komunikasi dan Multimedia 1998.
b9b652adff2ebc39: KUALA LUMPUR: Data centre projects in Malaysia have secured approval for 12.3 gigawatts (GW) of electricity supply capacity as of August, with the government projecting maximum demand from the sector to reach 8,391 megawatts by 2030.

Energy Transition and Water Transformation Minister Datuk Fadillah Yusof said the government was taking a phased approach to expanding power generation and strengthening grid infrastructure to support the industry's growth without compromising supply reliability.
He said the government was also working to ensure that additional costs arising from data centres' substantial electricity requirements were not unfairly passed on to other consumers.

In a written parliamentary reply to Syerleena Abdul Rashid (PH-Bukit Bendera), Fadillah said the government adopted an approach based on the principle of cost causation, under which parties responsible for additional system requirements or costs should bear the associated expenses fairly.

Measures introduced include the Ultra High Voltage tariff, which took effect on July 1, 2025, for existing and new data centres receiving electricity at high-voltage and extra-high-voltage levels. The tariff aims to ensure that infrastructure and electricity supply costs are borne more fairly by large-scale users.

The government has also increased the Connected Load Charge to encourage data centres to use their approved electricity capacity efficiently and discourage applications for capacity beyond actual requirements.

Fadillah said data centres must also use at least 30 per cent renewable energy based on their total electricity demand capacity. This requirement can be met through the Corporate Renewable Energy Supply Scheme and the Solar for Self-Consumption initiative.
The industry is also encouraged to develop its own electricity generation facilities to reduce complete dependence on the National Grid, he said.
He added that the Energy Commission was developing a comprehensive framework and guidelines for self-generation facilities, which would apply to data centres and other industries.

4a2e9d9e3a86b467: BEIT HANINA: The World Food Programme said Monday it would end monthly assistance to 500,000 people in Gaza due to a funding shortfall, despite acute needs in the war-battered Palestinian territory.
With the cutbacks, 1.1 million Palestinians in Gaza – still about half the population – will be receiving either food or cash assistance each month from the UN agency, in reduced amounts.

The World Food Programme said its efforts had mitigated the effects during a famine last year in Gaza – an evaluation of the situation disputed by Israel – and warned that conditions had not improved to the point that it can take away aid.

"This has been a lifeline. But now, rather than being able to sustain and scale up that assistance, we're actually having to reduce it," Shaun Hughes, the WFP country director, told AFP at the agency's office in east Jerusalem.
"And that's not because we don't have humanitarian access to deliver food; that's because we don't have funding."
According to the latest assessments, 1.4 million people – or two-thirds of Gaza's population – are still "acutely food insecure" and need humanitarian assistance to survive, he said.
Palestinians living in Gaza, where nearly the entire population has been displaced at least once, voiced alarm at the cuts in assistance.
"The hardest thing for a mother is to see her children hungry and be unable to provide food for them," said Samaher al-Najjar, 45, from the southern city of Khan Yunis.
"We live in a tent and do not have the money to buy everything we need. We rely on aid to provide part of our food," she said.
"All we want is for our children to have something to eat every day. The consequences of this would be extremely difficult."
Ayman Daghmash, 40, from Gaza City called news of the cutoffs "frightening."
"The assistance helped us get by for several days, but now we do not know how we will meet our family's needs, especially after community kitchens in Gaza stopped operating some time ago," he said.
"There is also no work or steady income, and food prices are beyond our means. If assistance stops coming from every direction, how will we feed our children?"
The WFP was able to bring in more assistance after a US-brokered ceasefire took effect a year ago. Israel has kept striking Gaza since then, vowing to kill anyone involved in the Oct 7 attack.
Between 1.5 million and 1.8 million people have been receiving assistance every month.
In addition to reducing the number of people who receive rations, the WFP will shrink the content.
Families receiving food assistance will now get only one food parcel instead of two and a smaller bag of wheat flour, the WFP said in an operational note.
The 75,000 families who receive assistance in cash will see the amount reduced from 1,250 to 750 shekels (US$400 to US$240) per month.
The WFP is funded by governments as well as private donors.
It has seen a sharp drop in resources, including after President Donald Trump returned to power in the United States and drastically slashed contributions to UN agencies, as well as bilateral aid.

The agency says it needs about US$450 million over the next six months for its operations in Gaza and the West Bank, but in 2026 it has only received about half the usual financing for the Palestinian territories.
In September, the agency also reduced by half the number of aid recipients in the West Bank, which Israel has occupied since 1967, from 400,000 to 200,000.

Israel has allowed more goods into Gaza under the terms of the Trump ceasefire, but still turns away shipments of anything that is seen as having potential military use – a policy that has included blocking even prosthetic limbs, according to the United Nations.
Israel has ramped up longstanding criticism of the United Nations since the Gaza war, accusing the world body of bias and perpetuating dependency among Palestinians.

d0e35f481b5c5c10: The proposed RM2,500 minimum wage for graduates under the 2027 Budget—slated for June next year—could be feasible. But if badly handled, it could be counter-productive.

The Malaysian Employers Federation, while agreeable to the new wage structure, suggested a thorough study before making it mandatory. The Human Resources Ministry is preparing basic salary guidelines.

So, how realistic is this RM2,500 minimum wage? At a glance, it is well-suited for technical and professional roles, such as engineering, semiconductors, banking and accounting, as well as information technology fields like artificial intelligence, software programming and data analytics.
Larger employers could accommodate this rate for their management trainee programmes. It is harder though, for small businesses, nonprofit organisations and cash-conscious start-ups.

A degree is no guarantee that a fresh graduate will immediately generate RM2,500 in economic value. However, employers should first recognise these qualifications and invest in developing inexperienced hires to ensure a fairer return on education and skills.
Economically, a guaranteed minimum wage provides relief as rising costs weigh heavily on fresh graduates.

Companies cannot exploit inexperienced and fresh graduates. The new floor wage should incentivise employers to invest in productivity, technology and skills development rather than relying on cheap labour.

Even so, the opposite could happen after June 2027. Some employers may shift away from hiring fresh degree holders—opting instead for diploma holders, experienced workers or those with postgraduate degrees—for entry-level roles.
Meanwhile, smaller companies unable to justify the higher starting salaries may cut graduate training positions altogether.
To circumvent the policy, companies may choose to automate tasks, delay expansion or turn to temporary and contract staff.

Current employees earning RM2,500 or more may demand higher salaries, increasing payroll costs. Graduates with limited experience may be priced out of their first jobs, thus defeating the policy's purpose.
The government may need to consider wider exemptions, particularly when the general RM2,000 minimum wage becomes a complicated framework.

While these risks are not inevitable, their outcome hinges on how the government designs the policy, which currently exempts companies with annual sales under RM50 million, alongside the overall wage floor.
The RM2,500 minimum wage, if implemented carefully, can improve income, make qualifications financially worthwhile and boost investment in skilled jobs.
Above all, the government must solve the mismatch between qualifications and actual skills required.
The policy's success may well depend on graduates securing productive roles and driving sustainable wage growth.
f6994e79a8c7c441: KUALA LUMPUR: Two female students were injured when their motorcycle collided with a Rapid KL bus on Jalan Ampang, near the Social Security Organisation (Perkeso) building.

4ce3f0612fe08097: YANGON: Myanmar's Aung San Suu Kyi received a package from Britain's King Charles III on Monday, authorities said, releasing the first pictures of the detained Nobel laureate in two months and describing her as a "special female prisoner".

It is the first time Myanmar authorities have used the term to describe Suu Kyi, who was deposed in a military coup in 2021, triggering an ongoing civil war that has killed more than 100,000 people, according to monitor ACLED.

The coup leader and former junta chief Min Aung Hlaing was installed as civilian president in April following elections that did not include Suu Kyi's party, and she was moved to house arrest soon afterwards.

Home ministry officials met her on Monday to deliver a package of two books about soil, "one sealed envelope, and a sealed diplomatic communication sent by King Charles III of the UK to the special female detainee", Myanmar's presidential spokeswoman said on her Facebook page.
Britain is Myanmar's former colonial power and the monarch is known to have a keen interest in gardening and the environment.
Accompanying the statement were two images of Suu Kyi meeting two men with their backs to the camera.

The pictures appeared to be in a similar room to the last released images of her, when she met a Red Cross representative in August, her first publicised meeting with a foreign official since her ouster.
Fact-checkers from AFP examined the latest photos and found no evidence of manipulation using Meta Generative AI or OpenAI tools.
Suu Kyi remains detained on charges rights groups say were concocted to return power to the military, which has historically ruled Myanmar since independence.
"I have been extremely lenient toward her," Min Aung Hlaing said in an interview with Time magazine published last month.
The Foreign Office in London did not immediately respond to questions from AFP asking whether British diplomats had sought to deliver the package in person, or been refused permission to do so.

072ee7c606cb4faa: OIL markets initially treated the Iran war as a brief bullish disruption in a long-term bearish trend. But traders are now betting that oil prices will remain elevated through 2028, forcing a rethink of the global inflation outlook.

Eight months into the war, the buffers that helped absorb the initial energy shock — most notably onshore crude oil stockpiles — are wearing dangerously thin. At the same time, the recovery in crude exports through the Strait of Hormuz remains fragile, global refining capacity has been eroded and credible diplomatic pathways to end the conflict appear narrower than ever.

Global benchmark Brent crude futures tell the story. Contracts for delivery in December next year have climbed more than 13 per cent since the start of September to US$86 a barrel, the highest level for the contract, while this December, contracts have gained around 12 per cent.

The Brent forward curve is not a price forecast, of course. But it reflects the willingness of refiners, airlines, commodity traders and asset managers to lock in elevated prices months and even years into the future.
In effect, market participants are paying a premium against the possibility that today's disruptions will become tomorrow's normal.
This market positioning stands in stark contrast to widely held industry expectations of a recovery in global oil supplies next year.
The International Energy Agency projects global supply will rise to 108.3 million barrels per day (bpd) next year from 100.7 million bpd this year as Middle Eastern exports recover.
Demand, meanwhile, is forecast to increase from 102.4 million bpd to 104.4 million bpd next year, still slightly below last year's consumption.
This recovery is expected to be concentrated in petrochemical feedstocks rather than transportation fuels like diesel.
Regardless, the agency's projected balances imply a sizeable supply surplus next year that would normally weigh on prices.
Yet the steady rise in long-dated futures suggests investors are increasingly sceptical that this recovery will fully materialise or, if it does, that it will endure.
The standoff between Washington and Teheran remains centred on control of the Strait of Hormuz.

The conflict has also expanded beyond the Gulf. Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis have recently stepped up missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia, including strikes last week on the headquarters of state-owned oil giant Aramco in Dhahran.
Given this backdrop, every barrel leaving the Gulf now carries a widening security premium.
Absent a durable settlement over Hormuz, much of that cost is likely to remain entrenched in prices for the foreseeable future.
The strain is even more visible in diesel markets.

Benchmark European diesel futures hit a record US$1,480 per metric tonne, equivalent to about US$210 per barrel, in mid-September amid an acute shortage of supplies caused by disruptions in the Middle East and Russia.
Since Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, drone attacks by Kyiv have crippled Russian refineries, forcing Moscow to ban diesel exports earlier this year.

On Friday, United States President Donald Trump announced an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin to allow Moscow to resume some diesel exports and later proclaimed another "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine.

But the additional Russian exports cited by Trump are minuscule — equivalent to roughly 12 hours of global supply — and no one, including the two parties involved, is giving much credence to the purported ceasefire.
Fuel repricing may ultimately prove more important than the rise in crude itself.

Diesel powers the trucks, ships, factories and farms that underpin global commerce. Sustained diesel inflation has historically seeped into the wider economy through higher transportation, manufacturing and food costs.
For much of this year, energy markets operated on the assumption that the Iran war would resemble past geopolitical crises: a sharp but temporary disruption followed by a quick return to normality.
Increasingly, investors are concluding otherwise. The issue is no longer simply how much oil can move through Hormuz.
Markets need to know whether the global energy system can quickly rebuild the inventories, refinery capacity and supply chains damaged by months of conflict.
Until then, the world risks becoming trapped in an era of structurally higher energy costs that lasts long after the shooting stops.
The writer is from Reuters

7cfbc233bb2d8747: AS doubts mount over Asia's artificial intelligence boom, some of the region's strongest returns are building far from the hype.
While tech dominates the headlines, old-economy mainstays are also key drivers of the broader market story.

Technology accounts for six of Asia's 15 best-performing market sectors this year thus far. But the remaining nine tell a non-tech story anchored in financials, energy, industrials and process industries.

Admittedly, some of these themes overlap with the AI capital expenditure juggernaut. For example, investments in power generation, grid infrastructure and industrial cooling are clearly being propelled by data centre needs.
But AI is not the only driver of these old-economy investment sweet spots, as geopolitical unrest and high energy prices are also playing a role.
Fears about a slowdown in the tech boom may rattle Asian markets—as we saw last week—but they will not necessarily bring the Asian surge to a screeching halt.
Rising global defence spending has been a major investment driver worldwide this year, as military tensions escalate, most notably in the Middle East and Europe.

This trend has been building ever since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and has skyrocketed as United States President Donald Trump has put more pressure on European allies to increase defence spending.

North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (Nato) members, which account for 65 per cent of global defence expenditure, committed in June last year to raise their annual defence spending to five per cent of gross domestic product by 2035. Global defence spending represented only 2.4 per cent of global GDP last year.
The widening conflict in the Middle East, which escalated following the US-Israeli strikes on Iran on Feb 28, has also highlighted the vulnerability of Gulf countries.

Asian defence manufacturers stand to gain from this global defence spending boom as Western capacity constraints potentially give Asian rivals an edge in delivery times and prices for comparable equipment.

According to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, South Korea supplied 8.6 per cent of all arms imported by European Nato members during 2021-2025, ahead of Israel's 7.7 per cent and France's 7.4 per cent.
This came as Europe's overall arms imports roughly tripled.
At the same time, "insourcing" of defence manufacturing—creating a homegrown military-industrial complex—is already a trend in several Asian nations.

India aims for 70 per cent defence "indigenisation" by next year, Indonesia seeks 60 per cent local content in defence equipment by 2030, and Vietnam is targeting 50 per cent domestic inputs in select armaments by 2030.

Increasing defence needs and military modernisation are also spurring a broader infrastructure buildout globally. This includes reinforced bridges, roads, ports and railways, which are needed to transport heavy equipment, alongside fortified energy grids, telecommunications services and cyber networks.
McKinsey forecasts US$106 trillion in global infrastructure investment through 2040, with Asia accounting for roughly 65 per cent of that.
The region's domestic industry has several advantages, including local ties, inexpensive state financing and integrated operations that can lower costs and speed delivery.

Asia's infrastructure buildout could be mammoth, too. Regional transport infrastructure alone could require investment of US$2.6 trillion annually through 2035, according to the Asian Transport Observatory and the Asian Development Bank.
The global drive for energy independence should also benefit Asia, the leader in clean energy technologies.

The stickiness of crude oil prices above US$100 a barrel—and the related shock closure of the Strait of Hormuz this year—should push more consumers, businesses and governments towards renewables, particularly solar power, battery energy storage, offshore wind and electric vehicles.

According to FactSet, Chinese electric vehicle makers BYD and Geely draw 43 per cent and 23 per cent of their respective revenue from abroad, while Chinese battery titan CATL generates 34 per cent of its revenue overseas.
Swapping AI exposure for heavy industry and state-backed defence does not eliminate risk—it merely trades tech valuation hype for other hazards.
Meanwhile, prolonged inflation, elevated energy prices and high interest rates could slow infrastructure buildouts and trigger corporate defaults.
And a truly massive AI pullback could have ripple effects across the region's markets.
Yet, for now, Asia's old economy continues to offer genuine substance beyond all the tech-driven hype.
Writing for Reuters, the writer is founder and CEO of Emmer Capital Partners Ltd

bbca3f6d57bce94a: KUALA LUMPUR: Three major shareholders of CTOS Digital Bhd have collectively disposed of nearly 22 million shares since Sept 23, when the credit reporting agency disclosed a cybersecurity breach that has since sent its share price tumbling.
Bursa Malaysia filings showed that the Employees Provident Fund (EPF), Retirement Fund Inc (KWAP) and Aberdeen Group plc have reported only disposals, with no acquisitions, during the period.
CTOS shares fell 15.29 per cent, or 6.5 sen, to close at a fresh record low of 36 sen on Monday (Oct 19), after hitting an intraday low of 35.5 sen.
The latest decline brings the stock's cumulative loss to 44.19 per cent from its Sept 22 closing price of 64.5 sen, the last trading day before the cybersecurity disclosure.
CTOS was the eighth most actively traded counter on Bursa Malaysia, with 29.39 million shares changing hands, its highest daily trading volume in over three months.
Of the three institutional shareholders, KWAP recorded the largest reduction in its holdings since Sept 23, followed by EPF and Aberdeen.
KWAP's latest disposal involved 1.77 million shares on Oct 16, reducing its stake to 191.81 million shares, or 8.724 per cent. Its holdings have declined by about 10.99 million shares.
EPF, meanwhile, disposed of 1.31 million shares on Oct 14, bringing its holdings to 449.10 million shares, or 20.43 per cent. Its holdings have fallen by about 6.38 million shares.

Aberdeen's latest reported disposal involved 384,000 shares on Oct 14, leaving it with 325.22 million shares, representing a 14.79 per cent stake. Its holdings have declined by about 4.20 million shares.
The combined reduction of about 21.57 million shares represents roughly one per cent of CTOS's issued share capital.
Meanwhile, CTOS itself bought back 500,000 shares at 61 sen apiece on Sept 25, two days after disclosing the cybersecurity breach, for an estimated RM305,000.
The stock has since fallen nearly 41 per cent from that repurchase price to today's closing price of 36 sen.
CTOS first disclosed the breach on Sept 23, saying unauthorised access had been detected in an environment supporting its consumer business.
The company said certain files containing a limited subset of processed consumer information had been accessed, although the incident had been contained and other systems were unaffected.
At the time, CTOS said the breach was not expected to have a material financial impact.

However, on Oct 13, the company estimated that the disruption would reduce its profit after tax and minority interests by RM12 million and revenue by RM16 million for the financial year ending Dec 31, 2026.
The estimates assumed that certain affected services, including CTOS Score and Central Credit Reference Information System-related reports, would remain unavailable until the third week of October.
CTOS also estimated that every additional week of disruption could reduce profit by RM1.3 million and revenue by RM2.5 million.
This has prompted several research houses to downgrade the stock and lower their earnings forecasts.
Hong Leong Investment Bank Bhd and CIMB Securities Sdn Bhd downgraded CTOS to "Hold" from "Buy", while Kenanga Research lowered its recommendation to "Market Perform" from "Outperform".
Kenanga adopted a more conservative assumption that the affected services could remain unavailable until the end of December, potentially raising the profit impact to RM22 million.
RHB Research, however, maintained its "Buy" recommendation, arguing that the sell-off had been excessive given CTOS's established position in the credit reporting industry.

Analysts have also raised concerns that restoring the affected services may not immediately translate into a recovery in transaction volumes, with potential customer migration and higher cybersecurity spending posing risks to future earnings.

The sharp decline in CTOS shares has also coincided with the appointment of Putri Norlisa Najib, the daughter of former prime minister Datuk Seri Najib Razak, as an independent non-executive director.
The stock gained one sen to close at 64.5 sen a day after her appointment was announced on Sept 21, before beginning its decline.

b89f4b2a881c721e: TEMERLOH: Police have arrested 17 men suspected of belonging to four gangs linked to robberies and cable theft involving the East Coast Rail Link (ECRL) project and Telekom Malaysia in Temerloh.

In an operation early today, four men aged between 22 and 31, believed to be members of Geng Mista, were arrested in Bukit Desa Semantan. Police seized a Mitsubishi Triton, several coils of cable, 27 cut sections believed to belong to Telekom Malaysia, and equipment used to pull and cut cables.

All four suspects had previous criminal and drug-related records and tested positive for methamphetamine. The gang's leader was also identified as a member of Geng Kepala, which was busted on Oct 14, while another suspect remains at large.

8dfa1cdd9d4ba5e7: KYIV: Ukraine received no advance warning from its partners of a Russian ballistic missile strike overnight, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Monday, adding that some vital deliveries from the United States were being delayed.

Railway and metro stations, pharmaceutical warehouses, commercial properties and residential buildings were also damaged, Koretskyi said.

"The aim is obvious — to wear people down," Koretskyi said.

b927d7f67bd56d39: LONDON: Microsoft confirmed Monday that it has pulled out of a UK AI data centre deal with British start-up Nscale, in a blow to the country's artificial intelligence (AI) ambitions.

The US technology giant agreed last year to lease computing capacity from AI infrastructure provider Nscale, which is backed by chip titan Nvidia, at a planned data centre in Loughton, northeast of London.
A Microsoft spokesman said "this decision relates to a single site", adding the company remains "committed to our partnership with Nscale".

"We remain committed to both the Loughton project and the UK and we are exploring alternative power sources for the site, in addition to other expansion sites in the UK," an Nscale spokesman said Monday.
"Our relationship with Microsoft remains strong and long-term, and this unfortunate London-wide grid issue has no impact on our other contracts," they added.
UK media reported that power grid officials had told Nscale that the site would not have access to power until the 2030s.
It comes as Nscale gears up for an initial public offering on the New York Stock Exchange, reportedly targeting a valuation of up to US$35 billion.

UK Power Networks, which does not disclose information about individual connections, told AFP on Monday that "many data centres, whilst they can connect to our distribution network, are awaiting works on the national transmission network, which we do not own".
63e3d371f946e001: PARIS: France's prime minister called for partial curfews Monday as protesters blocked the entrance to the Louvre in Paris and authorities scrambled to stem public discontent fuelling cost-of-living demonstrations that over the weekend spilled over into some of the worst street violence in recent years.

Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu did not rule out imposing a state of emergency after the interior minister said the police "had lost control" during the weekend's unrest, which has flared six months before France elects a successor to President Emmanuel Macron.

With organisers calling for a new round of protests next Saturday, Lecornu called for regional authorities to impose "partial" curfews to protect businesses and people after hundreds of shops were damaged and looted.
"I'm absolutely determined to restore public order", he said, adding that the government was ready to impose a state of emergency "if needed."

Other European countries, where anger over rising prices has also led to protests, were keeping a nervous eye on the developments, with smaller clashes breaking out in Milan, Italy's financial capital, and Belgium over the weekend and protests simmering in Spain and Portugal.

Some half a million people turned out across France on Saturday to denounce the surging cost of living, a culmination of four weeks of protests that began with high school students demanding better conditions at their schools.

What started as peaceful demonstrations morphed into violence in some places, as masked groups on the sidelines of the protests attacked law enforcement, broke into town halls and other public buildings, setting many of them ablaze, looted shops, and set fire to cars, bicycles and scooters on the streets.
More than 2,500 people were arrested and nearly 1,000 members of the security forces injured. Protesters were also hurt, with one demonstrator's hand blown off by a police crowd-control grenade.
"On Saturday, in some major cities, you couldn't look shopkeepers in the eye after hundreds of shops had been looted and tell them we hadn't lost control," Nunez said.
He said "a number of measures" aimed at containing and preventing looters and vandals would be implemented "starting this evening", including boosting police on the streets.
Macron acknowledged failures in the government response, despite the deployment of some 60,000 law enforcement personnel across the country on Saturday.

Nationwide, more than 2,330 people were taken into police custody over the weekend, 70 percent of whom were adults – and many of whom were already known to authorities, said Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said.
At least 3,000 businesses were affected by the unrest, according to Trade and Small Businesses Minister Serge Papin, with damage running into hundreds of millions of euros.
In an address to the nation Sunday, Macron slammed the "unbridled" violence and said local authorities would be able to ban some rallies, but stopped short of imposing more drastic measures.
City authorities in the southern port city of Marseille said they had banned public gatherings from noon to 8pm (1000-1800 GMT).
The European Union slammed the weekend violence as "unacceptable" but warned that the right to peaceful protest "must be protected" in France.
Germany condemned the violence and updated its travel advice for France, saying "further demonstrations and, in some cases, further outbreaks of violence in the coming days cannot be ruled out."
The United Kingdom said the right to protest "can never excuse violence."
In Paris on Monday, about a dozen demonstrators blocked the entrance to the iconic Louvre Museum, the most visited in the world, while puzzled tourists looked on.
"We don't want to get involved. We want to stand back and get away from them," Pat Boland, a tourist from Australia, said of the protests.
"But we don't want to go against them either," his wife Anne added.

The two pensioners, both 73, spoke to AFP outside barricades that had been erected at the Louvre, which had closed as a small group of protesters occupied an area outside its famed glass pyramid entrance.

Rising prices have fuelled anger in France, where diesel prices have jumped nearly 40 per cent and petrol by 25 per cent since March, and where food prices have risen by 25 per cent over the past five years.

The unrest has flared just months before presidential elections that will see a new French president elected after a decade of centrist Macron and with Marine Le Pen, the far-right presidential candidate for the National Rally party, riding high in the polls.
Ministers and Le Pen have accused ultra-left groups of stoking the violence to boost the chances of the far-left firebrand Jean-Luc Melenchon in the presidential polls.
On Monday, Lecornu blamed the "ultra-left movement" for seeking to "orchestrate deep unrest across the country."
"There is a whole network that could be mobilised to even call into question the timetable for the presidential election and the holding of the presidential election itself," Lecornu told reporters.
Melenchon said he was "astonished" at the remarks and said he had "not heard anyone talk about that."

"I'm very worried because it's a new phenomenon, which also originates from an international scenario and therefore feeds itself," Mayor Giuseppe Sala said.
In Belgium, police fired tear gas and water cannon to disperse protesters in Brussels and Liege.
In Spain protesters have set up tents in the heart of Madrid to denounce soaring housing costs, with similar encampments going up in neighbouring Portugal's main cities of Lisbon and Porto.

a88be2626f8f70d5: KUALA LUMPUR: The government has made no agreement or commitment to provide financial support to low-cost carrier AirAsia amid financial difficulties linked to the Middle East conflict, Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim said.

Anwar, who is also finance Mminister, said any application for government support from a company in any sector was considered based on the interests of the country and the people, the government's fiscal sustainability and the protection of public funds, in accordance with applicable laws and procedures.
"To date, the government has made no agreement or commitment to provide financial support to AirAsia, whether in the form of guarantees, loans or injections of public funds.

"The government will not comment on speculation or figures reported by the media to avoid affecting the market and the interests of employees, customers and other stakeholders of the companies concerned," he said in a written parliamentary reply published on Parliament's website today.
He was responding to Datuk Seri Dr Wee Ka Siong (BN-Ayer Hitam), who asked whether the government was considering providing financial support to the AirAsia Group.

Anwar said the government continuously monitored developments in the country's aviation ecosystem, including the impact of the Middle East crisis, global fuel prices and currency movements on airlines and air connectivity for the people.

He added that the government took note of the issues raised concerning AirAsia, including the losses reported in its latest quarterly financial results, which the low-cost carrier attributed mainly to a sharp increase in jet fuel prices following developments in the Middle East conflict.

"AirAsia is an important part of this ecosystem. In 2025, AirAsia accounted for about 41 per cent of the 104.5 million passenger movements at airports operated by Malaysia Airports Holdings Bhd and nearly 60 per cent of domestic passenger movements.
"Much of the air connectivity in Sabah and Sarawak depends on AirAsia flights.
"In 2025, AirAsia carried 62 per cent and 70 per cent of total passengers in Sabah and Sarawak respectively, excluding short take-off and landing (STOL) ports.
"At KLIA Terminal 2, AirAsia carried three-quarters of all passengers," he said.

Transport Minister Anthony Loke had previously said that no meeting had been held between his ministry and AirAsia in the past "two or three weeks" amid speculation about potential government support for the low-cost carrier.
However, Loke said any discussions on the matter might have involved the Finance Ministry.
194b54a08932ad8c: JAKARTA: Polis Indonesia mengesahkan penglibatan pihak asing, termasuk dari negara jiran, dalam kes korporat berkaitan kebakaran hutan dan tanah, dengan 98 kes kini dalam siasatan.

Suyudi berkata penyiasat sedang mengumpul bukti dan dijangka menamakan suspek tidak lama lagi, termasuk pemilik syarikat dan pemegang saham yang boleh dipertanggungjawabkan atas kebakaran itu.

Dudung turut berkata Indonesia telah memberi maklum balas terhadap tawaran bantuan luar, termasuk daripada Malaysia dan Singapura, dengan Badan Nasional Pengurusan Bencana (BNPB) menyelaras pengaturan teknikal bagi cadangan sokongan berkenaan.

Bagaimanapun, beliau pada sidang media terdahulu berkata bantuan luar perlu menunggu sehingga kerajaan mengisytiharkan kebakaran itu sebagai bencana nasional, satu langkah yang belum diambil memandangkan Indonesia masih berupaya mengendalikan krisis berkenaan menggunakan sumber sendiri.

796b2939b776c67e: KUALA LUMPUR: Is the FA of Malaysia (FAM) getting leaner and meaner by booting out some of its staff?

f448ec62808d8b06: PETALING JAYA: Kerajaan tidak membuat persetujuan atau komitmen untuk memberi sebarang bentuk bantuan kepada syarikat penerbangan tambang rendah, AirAsia, yang berdepan masalah kewangan susulan kesan konflik di Timur Tengah, kata Perdana Menteri, Anwar Ibrahim.

2ba983b98533fe07: Uber has dodged a £340 million lawsuit brought by thousands of London black cab drivers after a High Court judge ruled that they'd left it too late to sue. Monday's ruling kills off two claims involving around 13,000 cabbies and former private hire companies Kabbee and Iride, which accused Uber of misleading Transport for London (TfL) to secure its operating license. The cabbies wanted nearly £200 million in compensation for lost earnings, while Kabbee and Iride sought another £140 million. But the court never got as far as deciding whether Uber had done anything wrong. The claims were filed in May and June 2024, but Mr Justice Simon Birt ruled they were too late under the six-year time limit. The cabbies insisted that they hadn't had enough evidence to allege fraud until June 2018, but the judge wasn't buying it. According to the judgment, seen by The Register, three cabbies had already filed their own claims against Uber in September 2017. Litigation funder Harbour approached law firm Mishcon de Reya about a larger lawsuit that December, and by February 2018, the Licensed Taxi Drivers' Association was telling members about the planned action. The dispute dates back to Uber's arrival in London in 2012. The claimants alleged that the company deliberately misled TfL about how its booking system worked, allowing it to operate when it shouldn't have been permitted to do so. Uber has some history here. In a separate licensing appeal in 2018, the company admitted that it gave TfL and the High Court false information about how bookings were accepted through its app. The magistrate stopped short of finding dishonesty, however, and granted Uber a new 15-month license. The judgment also revisits Greyball, Uber's software for identifying suspected regulators, and Ripley, a tool used to remotely lock computers during regulatory visits. Uber maintained that Ripley hadn't been used that way in the UK. The cabbies insisted that they needed information from the June 2018 licensing appeal to support their fraud allegations. Justice Birt disagreed, finding that enough information had been available earlier to bring a claim. Things then went quiet. Mishcon sent Uber a letter before action in July 2019, but Harbour pulled its funding that November. The claimants didn't write to Uber again about the potential lawsuit for another four and a half years, according to the judgment, and by the time proceedings began in 2024, the deadline had passed. The ruling is a victory for Uber, but doesn't clear it of the alleged fraud. The judge dismissed the claims because they were filed too late, without deciding whether the allegations, which Uber denies, were true. Neither Uber nor RGL Management, the company representing the cabbies, responded to The Register’s questions. London's taxi wars are far from over. Minicab Drivers are now pushing back against plans to bring robotaxis to the capital, warning that driverless cars could put thousands of jobs at risk. Uber is working with British autonomous driving startup Wayve on driverless technology. Having spent years battling London's cabbies for passengers, it's now helping develop cars that won't need drivers at all. ®

In the past few years, Character.AI has faced multiple private lawsuits over the safety of its chatbots, as well as investigations from regulators around the world.
