3b5e3f0ff2498c74: PETALING JAYA: Eight packages of the Pan Borneo Highway in Sabah stretching 177km in total will open in stages before the year ends, says deputy chief minister Dr Joachim Gunsalam.
Joachim, the state works minister, said improvements will be carried out by the Sabah government after the auditor-general's report released two weeks ago flagged multiple issues with the project.
"Our focus now is to resolve the issues raised so that the people can use the highway as soon as possible," he said, according to Berita Harian.

As of Sept 25, eight packages spanning 41.5km have been fully completed, comprising sections connecting Papar to Donggongon, Tawau to Semporna, the Lahad Datu Bypass, and Kampung Lot M to Sandakan Mile 32.
Six packages involving 135.8km have received certificates of partial occupation, connecting Sindumin to Beaufort, Bongawan-Putatan to Tebobon, and Moynod to Sapi Nangoh.
Meanwhile, eight other packages that make up 161.8km of the highway are expected to receive certificates of practical completion next year.

Yesterday, Joachim said the claim in the auditor-general's report that the project was only 11.4% complete did not reflect actual progress on the ground as it only measured fully handed-over packages.
He said other packages were actively being built, with some alignments recording between 90% and 93% physical progress.

The issues highlighted by the report have led to an investigation by the Public Accounts Committee into the management, financial governance, and physical implementation of the Pan Borneo project in Sabah.

3d2cf87c0c103bc6: About a month ago, a Chinese rocket took off from a remote spaceport in the Gobi Desert, released 10 satellites into orbit, then reignited its engine and put itself on a trajectory to rain down debris over the American Midwest.

The rocket's flight on September 15 lasted between 75 and 80 minutes, and it came down without completing a full orbit of the Earth. Social media posts at the time showed streaks of fiery debris falling from the sky, heading north over Kansas toward Minnesota. The overnight spectacle was also visible on the western horizon from Wisconsin.

The exact time, location, and direction of the debris allowed experts to connect it to the launch of a Zhuque-2E rocket, a medium-lift vehicle built by a Chinese company called LandSpace. The rocket had launched from Dongfeng, a commercial launch zone co-located with the military-run Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwestern China, less than two hours before.

99c5023d5ecdf0df: Today, I’m talking with Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, who has a lot of thoughts about AI, tech, and privacy.

If you’ve been listening to the show, you know that one of my running theories is that those issues are driving a big and maybe kind of unexpected political realignment — and with the midterms coming up next month, and early voting already underway in a lot of places, the stakes are pretty high right now.

So I asked Gov. Pritzker about all that, and he was surprisingly willing to dive right into the absolute existential weeds of what government is even for. You’ll hear him say — and it’s hard to disagree — that some problems are just collective action problems that require the government to do a lot of work. We can’t solve all these problems one at a time, or even one state at a time. It’s a pretty deep conversation, and we really got into it on a lot of issues.
And of course, I had to ask him: Are the Bears gonna stay in Illinois?
Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday.
Okay: Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker. Here we go.
Gov. JB Pritzker, you’re the governor of Illinois. Welcome to Decoder.
Thanks, Nilay. Great to be with you.

I am very excited to talk to you. We’re in the heart of midterm season. You are running for reelection. I have to tell you. I have to be very honest with you. I personally feel a lot of pressure in this interview, not only because I’m speaking to a governor, but because I went to school in Chicago. My sister still lives in Chicago. My wife grew up in Illinois. Her entire family is farmers in North Central Illinois. Boy, do I have a list of questions for you. I have to do a good job here.
Well, we’re claiming you. Now that I know all that, we’re claiming you. You’re an Illinoisan.
Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.
I don’t know about that. I grew up in Wisconsin. Here’s my first question for you. I’m a die-hard Packers fan. Are you going to let the Bears move to Indiana?
That is not our intention. We are, in fact, in discussions with the Bears and the NFL about keeping the Bears either in Chicago or in Arlington Heights, but in Illinois.

I’m saying, as a Packers fan, nothing is funnier than the outcome of the Bears moving to Indiana. I just want to put that out there. Openly biased in this case — I own two shares of that stock — but I’m going to make the comparison here. And the reason I started there is not only because I think that’s a funny outcome, although I do, but it feels like we are in the middle of a generational political realignment.

I’m sure you feel that, in this election campaign, the idea of big business and how that should interact with the government, and how the government should be able to push back on big business and not give in to big business. All of that feels up for grabs.

And the comparison I will make in this specific case is your fellow governor, Gavin Newsom, in California. They sued the Ellison family, Paramount, over the Warner Brothers merger. Paramount threatened to leave. They made a lot of noise about Nashville, Texas, Miami, or wherever you make noise about these days, and it feels like Newsom caved. It feels like he pressured his Attorney General, Rob Bonta, to settle that lawsuit and keep them there.

They settled the lawsuit. The next day, the Ellison family is like, “We never… We’re from California. We would never leave.” I see a parallel here with the Bears that is connected to that larger realignment, how government and business should interact. Do you see that parallel? Do you feel that realignment?

Well, what I can tell you is we’re pretty tough negotiators in Chicago and Illinois, and that’s really what we’re in the midst of now with the Bears. But I understand your point about realignment. I mean, there is a generational change, and I think it’s also an attitudinal change about protecting taxpayers, protecting people who frankly are among the most vulnerable to all the technology that’s overtaking people’s lives and invading people’s homes.

And so I do believe that the government has to be more active now and become a fighter for our people and not just a collaborator with business on everything. I’m a businessman, as you know, before I became governor. But I also know that, for the people of Illinois anyway, my job is to protect the working people of this state who often don’t have anybody protecting them except a government that will stand up for them. So that’s kind of the realignment that I see.

And that generational shift, I agree with you. It’s partly a Democratic Party generational shift. Generationally, we’re a little more aggressive. And I’m probably older than the next generation that’s already possibly taking office this November. I’m 61 years old, but I think of myself as having come out of the tech world and as somebody who has been a fighter for progressive values that, yeah, we’ve got to become more aggressive and make sure we’re standing up for our people.

There are two places where I see the realignment in particular. One is data centers, one is privacy, and you just see that as a bipartisan backlash to those things. I would actually add a third, which is antitrust broadly. It’s weird if you go into Silicon Valley. David Sacks is retweeting Lina Khan from the Biden administration talking about whether the AI industry needs an antitrust exemption to manage safety.

They both agree that these companies don’t need antitrust exemptions. They actually should be more competitive. Again, putting that in the context of regulating these companies, thinking about the dynamic between the government and the biggest companies in the world. I’ll just ask the question, I guess, more directly. Do you think Newsom was right to give in to Paramount, or do you think he should have forced them to make good on that threat to leave?

I can’t speak to the Paramount situation well enough to give you an answer, so it would be unfair for me to do so. I can say once again that our orientation today — and I think about the big AI companies and the big social media companies as well — has to be like, wait a minute, too much power in too few hands.

Particularly when we talk about AI, where it’s potentially existential, but certainly transformative, which is probably a kind way to say it about the economy, that we’re going to have to get very engaged. Guardrails, of course, on both parts, but also addressing what I think on the AI front is potentially a significant change in employment in the United States. I’m not somebody who is necessarily convinced that we have to see a whole bunch of job loss, but that does feel like that’s the direction this is going.

What I’m suggesting is we better be prepared, and we better be protecting people who are going to lose their jobs, or at least it appears they’re going to lose their jobs. And I’ll just give you this thought. If these days 4 percent unemployment is kind of the acceptable near full employment number, I think the problem we’re going to see is — if that’s sort of the level that we’re going to hopefully aim for and stay at — that in very short order, we could end up at 7 percent and have that be the baseline, or maybe 10 percent.

And if you think about what’s happened, the upheavals of economies and of governments when you get to 10 percent unemployment in any country. We better be focused on how we’re going to give people the dignity of work and enough income so that they can make a life for themselves when you’re going to put people out of work by virtue of this technology. By the way, much of the benefit of that is going to go to a very, very few people. So we’ve got to wrestle with that and come to a conclusion.

I wanted to start with some of the brinksmanship we have seen in the negotiations between, particularly, states and the big companies, because that brinksmanship is real. The threat is we will leave. We just covered, I don’t know, Kevin O’Leary in Utah talking about data centers, and the people of Utah really pushed back against Kevin O’Leary building that data center. But his argument was, “Well, I’m just going to shop around.”

This is what states do. They compete with tax incentives and benefits, maybe for data centers, which will put everyone out of a job. They compete for land use rights. You’ve got a rural state with a lot of farms in it. How are you thinking about that dynamic? Do you feel like you’re in competition with the other states, or is this bipartisan realignment creating more of a level playing field where these companies are going to have to actually give something?

We are in competition. We just are because it isn’t bipartisan, at least if you ask me. Unless there is a change in the government. I’ll pick on Texas for a second, and there is a chance that you’ll see a new governor in Texas as of November 3rd. In fact, a good chance. But if you look at Texas as it’s run today by a three-term, hoping to be a four-term, Republican governor and a Republican legislature, they have no intention of changing their alignment about incentives.

In the state of Illinois, we don’t want to have to do that. I mean, we obviously want to protect the revenue that we’ve got for the state to pay for the things we think are valuable to our people, but we also want to make sure that we’re attracting jobs and not losing jobs. And in a world where South Carolina, Michigan, Texas, Florida — pick your poison. Michigan may be slightly different just because it’s got democratic control, but these are our competitors. When I’m competing to have a company move to Illinois, I’ve got to make sure, first of all, that I’m somewhere in the ballpark when it comes to the incentives, because otherwise we don’t even get considered.

And then when I say somewhere in the ballpark, I mean, I want to give away less than more, and then I want to provide whatever other advantages I can that aren’t financial so that I can protect the resources that we have. An example of that is, we like to talk about a kind of white-glove service that we offer to companies. If you’re going to bring a factory here, let’s say, just to give an example, we want to make sure that we’ve got somebody who’s kind of a concierge for your company that’s walking you through each of our departments where you need a permit. It doesn’t mean we’re lowering the standards. It just means, a lot of times, the bureaucracy eats up so much time that it makes it impossible for a company to actually do what they want to do in your state.

We try to make sure that if we’re going to attract a large company, with 1,000, 2,000, 3,000 jobs, that we’re at least making it a little easier for them to go through without having to give them massive tax incentives. So that’s the way I think about it. We are in competition. There’s just no doubt about it. Should we be? There’s a lot of discussion about whether we shouldn’t, and maybe at the federal level we should do something about leveling the playing field, but this is the world we’re living in right now.

I wanted to ask those questions just to set the baseline. I really do think something is happening. A lot of young people are dissatisfied with the status quo. A lot of people in general are dissatisfied with what big tech companies are trying to do with AI, with the potential for job loss.

And the relationship between the people, the government, and those companies seems more fraught than ever, especially as they’re trying to expand their physical infrastructure with data centers, as they all become defense contractors, literally taking our tax dollars to sell weapon systems and collect data for the government. That’s a big swirl.

I wanted to start there, but I just want to take one second here and ask you the Decoder questions because I personally think the operation of government is so opaque. It’s very easy to figure out how big companies are run. The CEOs won’t shut up. They’re on podcasts all day long. I think most people have no idea how your job works.
So you were elected governor. How is your office set up, and how have you structured the state government of Illinois?

Just starting from where I sit, and then, of course, we look at it from a customer service perspective. But starting just at the top, I actually did something that no governor of Illinois has ever done — which is that I created not just one deputy governor. We obviously have a lieutenant governor who’s elected also, but a deputy governor is somebody getting appointed by me to serve under me, to help manage the government with me. What I did was put four deputy governors in place, a general counsel, and my chief of staff.

Why is that important? Because what I’ve tried to do is to break down the silos of government. I took all of the health and human services-related departments — that’s the Department of Public Health, the Department of Human Services, the Department of Healthcare and Family Services, everything from health insurance, Medicaid, and public health during the pandemic — and put it all under one deputy governor working directly for me. The idea is that instead of my having, let’s say, 26 direct reports, I’ve got four or five direct reports plus my chief of staff, who each have, let’s say, six or seven departments underneath them.

From my perspective, what I wanted to do was make sure that I’m breaking down the silos of government, making these departments that are often building walls, and they don’t want to talk to one another because they’re afraid they might lose jobs in one department to another department, or lose control of a program if they’re talking to one another. That’s the way it used to be. Now we’re like the deputy governor is there to either beat the heads together or at least bring them together so that they will be operating the government more efficiently. Okay, so that’s from the top.

From the bottom, which is: how do people who live in Illinois interact with the state government? And obviously, technology is one of the upgrades that’s occurred and made it easier. Illinois, frankly, had not significantly invested in those processes before I became governor, or in the technology that was necessary. And I’ll just give you one example of this: We created something called BEACON, which is designed to address the problem that parents and families have with mental health for children. It turns out that there were seven different ways in which people approached the government to get help, and we weren’t coordinating those, and we weren’t helping to provide all of the resources.

I’m talking about outside resources. How do you find a therapist? How do you find a psychiatrist? And how do you pay for those things? Medicaid, if you can’t afford it on your own. But the point is, there’s one door to enter through BEACON that allows you to get access to all of those resources, even if they’re in multiple departments. So that’s just one example. We’re trying to think of this as a customer service operation. It’s one thing to say this is how the org chart looks and another thing to say, this is how you access all the resources of the government that you need.

We provide programs that really matter to people. We have a birth equity initiative to reduce maternal mortality, particularly in Black and Brown communities. And free diapers for some people. The problem is, people don’t even know that the programs exist, and how would you ever figure out that the programs exist, especially if you’re a working person who’s working two minimum-wage jobs? You don’t have any time, and you don’t have any money, and you don’t even know how to talk to the government. And so we’re trying to fix all of those problems of the government with the way that we interact with people.

It’s funny. It feels like that is one of the bigger opportunities when it comes to AI, just letting the AI navigate a bureaucracy for you and communicate what resources are available. The flip side of that is that people hate AI. They truly dislike it, and it doesn’t feel like that connection has been made — that a lot of these tools can actually just navigate a bureaucracy for you. Are you thinking that should be an investment that you make, that it might be what turns the tide in terms of how people feel about these tools?
Yes, but I’m not plunging headlong into it. And I realize that there are probably states that are plunging headlong into it.
I mean, the United States government rolled out its AI chatbot to look at webpages across the government.
Well, there you go.

I guess what I’m trying to do is make sure that… I created something called the AI Cabinet in my government, and that is to essentially bring the experts on AI together with the leaders of my mainstay agencies of state government, so that we’re thinking about privacy, safety, and efficiency. And those things have to be talked about together. You can’t just say we’re going after efficiency and we don’t really care about the other two.

So that’s the idea, the AI cabinet. It’s also that, honestly, there are things, as you know, about AI that are dangerous. And so we’ve got our emergency management agency on that AI cabinet. We’ve got our state police on that AI cabinet. And remember, a lot of the people that work in those agencies aren’t particularly proficient at AI or really understand the potential and the potential dangers.

That’s why we brought in experts, for example, from the University of Chicago, the University of Illinois, just as two examples of places where we’re drawing expertise. So yeah, there’s a lot to be done. I would say we’re trying to approach it carefully before it gets out of control to a point where we have no way to pull it back in.

The other Decoder question I ask everybody is about decisions. You have a big job. You have some constraints in your decision-making process, right? There’s a state legislature, there’s a federal government, you have other agencies in your state. How do you make decisions? What’s your framework?
Well, I don’t do it the way Donald Trump does.

It’s funny you say it that way. I guess I start with the idea that we have a problem to solve and that decisions have to get made. Are those decisions ones that need to come to the governor? Because you’re right, I only have so much bandwidth. So the question is: which are the most serious ones that can’t be solved by other people, or are unlikely to get the outcomes that I would want by handing them over to other people? And then those automatically come to me.

So what I’m making decisions about is kind of the first answer to your question, and then it’s how do I actually make the decisions? For me, I am not one of those people who thinks that I’m right 100 percent of the time. Maybe a good way to describe it, and I’m joking a little bit when I say it, is that I’m 90 percent sure I’m right, but there’s also a 10 percent chance that I’m dead wrong. I want to make sure that I’m getting input and a debate before I actually make the final decision.

Someone once told me that the best CEOs are ones that, in their organization, are a little bit below average in terms of their capability and intellect. I’m not saying we want below-average leaders. I’m just saying you’re so good at hiring that you’ve got people in your organization who are really far better than you are at various things that you’re not particularly good at. Maybe knowing what you don’t know and being willing to ask for help is a philosophy that I have. Be willing to ask for help if it’s something you really don’t know.

ba9c774899cd8552: SINGAPORE: Singapore’s government issued notices to three more Indonesian firms suspected to be linked to haze-creating fires, as it steps up action to combat its worst air pollution in more than a decade.

PT Buana Megatama Jaya, PT Mananjung Hayak and PT Baratama Putra Perkasa will all be notified under the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act, Singapore’s National Environment Agency said in a statement today.
"There are indications that smoke from fires on concessions held by all three companies in Kalimantan spread to the city-state," the agency said.

Singapore and Malaysia have been blanketed by toxic smog from the Indonesian wildfires in recent weeks, with the dry conditions that have exacerbated the blazes linked to a powerful El Niño weather pattern.
Singapore prime minister Lawrence Wong last week vowed to investigate companies responsible for the blazes and warned that those found culpable could face legal action.
The action on Monday follows notices sent to seven companies on Friday.
"The notified firms will be required to deploy firefighters to curb blazes on their concessions," the agency said.
Under the transboundary haze law, Singaporean authorities can fine companies as much as S$100,000 (US$78,000) per day of pollution.
Buana Megatama Jaya is listed as a supplier to APP Group, one of the pulp and paper industry’s largest companies. Two of the companies notified on Friday were also suppliers to APP.
APP Group said in a written response that the notices issued by Singapore were preventive measures and did not constitute a finding of wrongdoing.

The pulp and paper giant said it would work with relevant suppliers to contain fires, prevent further outbreaks and enforce its zero-burning policy, adding that it had invested nearly US$300 million in fire management over the past decade.
Buana Megatama Jaya could not be reached for comment. Mananjung Hayak and Baratama Putra Perkasa didn’t immediately respond to emails seeking comment.
The 24-hour Pollutant Standards Index reading — which the act tracks — was as high as 114 on Monday after, according to NEA data.
That’s lower than last week, when levels in parts of the city topped 200.
In Pangkalanbun, a town in Kalimantan, a gauge of particulate matter peaked at more than 1,000 on Monday, figures from the Indonesian meteorology agency show. Levels above 250 are deemed dangerous.

Singapore also sought to enforce the transboundary haze law in 2015, but the environment ministry said at the time it was having difficulty getting information from its Indonesian counterpart on firms suspected of illegal burning.
A decade on, four companies continue to be under investigation.

75c70b6471aec7f3: PETALING JAYA: The government has not agreed to give low-cost carrier AirAsia any form of assistance amid financial struggles caused by the effects of the Middle East conflict, says Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim.
Anwar, who is also the finance minister, acknowledged reports of AirAsia's massive losses caused by the surge in jet fuel prices.

He said the government held periodical engagements with aviation industry players to get their views on the impact of the Middle East crisis, the same way it does with stakeholders in other affected sectors.
"Any request for government support from a company in any sector will be considered based on national interests, fiscal sustainability and the protection of public funds.

"For now, the government has not made any agreement or commitment to offer financial support to AirAsia, whether in the form of guarantees, loans or injection of public funds," he said in a written parliamentary reply to Wee Ka Siong (BN-Ayer Hitam).
Wee had asked whether the government would consider assisting AirAsia amid its financial issues.
Anwar said the government will continue to monitor developments in AirAsia and will not comment on speculation reported by the media.

Reuters previously reported that AirAsia was seeking to raise up to US$1 billion (RM4.08 billion) from international debt markets and secure RM700 million in local credit facilities, primarily to refinance existing debt.
AirAsia operated 66% of East Malaysia flights in 2025

The prime minister nonetheless pointed out that AirAsia played a crucial role in providing air connectivity to Sabah and Sarawak, serving 66% of flights to and from the East Malaysian states last year.
He said the airline handled 62% of Sabah's air travellers in 2025 and 70% of Sarawak's, except for short take-off and landing airports.
"Airports with the highest percentage of AirAsia passengers in both states were Sibu (79%), Bintulu (77%), Sandakan (75%), Kuching (72%), Tawau (70%), Miri (63%) and Kota Kinabalu (62%).
"In Peninsular Malaysia, states with the highest percentage of AirAsia passengers last year were Johor (70%), Terengganu (56%), Kedah (56% in Langkawi and 49% in Alor Setar), and Kelantan (46%).
“At KLIA Terminal 2, AirAsia flew three-quarters of the total passengers handled," he said.
Nationally, Anwar said the low-cost carrier handled 41% of the 104.5 million passengers at airports across the country, with nearly 60% domestic travellers.

ce54d9f17bd34408: PARIS: French prime minister Sebastien Lecornu said on Monday that a state of emergency could be imposed "if needed", while adding that curfews were a better solution to the crisis over violent protests.
With six months to go before France elects a successor to president Emmanuel Macron, the country was rocked over the weekend by some of its worst street violence in years.
The unrest came after weeks of student demonstrations demanding better conditions in schools.
"I am absolutely determined to restore order," Lecornu said after a crisis meeting, adding he did not rule out imposing a state of emergency.
"If needed, I will do it," he said.
"As things stand, however, the issue of curfews, and the implementation of those curfews, seems better suited to the situation we may be facing," he added.
In France, a state of emergency grants authorities temporary powers that go beyond ordinary policing in order to respond to a serious threat to public order or national security.
Measures can include curfews, restrictions on movement, and bans on public demonstrations.
Lecornu said he had asked regional authorities to impose "localised" curfews on Monday evening, notably to protect businesses.
A map of the curfew zones was set to be released later Monday following consultations with mayors.
"Watching television, the French get the impression that it's chaos everywhere. Fortunately, that's not the case," Lecornu said. "The disorder is highly concentrated in urban centres."
At least 3,000 businesses were affected by the unrest, according to trade and small businesses minister Serge Papin.
"They will benefit from a 'dedicated support fund' as well as other measures," Lecornu said.
Interior minister Laurent Nunez earlier Monday submitted his resignation, saying police had "lost control" in some cities at the weekend. Macron did not accept his resignation.
Standing next to Lecornu, Nunez said that "a number of measures" aimed at containing and preventing looters and vandals would be implemented "starting this evening".
"We will further increase the number of police officers and gendarmes deployed on the ground," he added.
Lecornu also accused the "ultra-left movement" of seeking to "orchestrate deep unrest across the country" in the runup to next spring's election.
"There is a whole network that could be mobilised to even call into question the timetable for the presidential election and the holding of the presidential election itself," he said.
f724f6808a4b2f7f: PETALING JAYA: Perbendaharaan meluluskan dana tambahan RM500 juta kepada Kementerian Kemajuan Desa dan Wilayah (KKDW) yang diterajui Timbalan Perdana Menteri, Zahid Hamidi selepas kementerian itu berbelanja melebihi peruntukan asal bagi tahun ini.

Menteri Kewangan, Anwar Ibrahim, berkata KKDW telah diperuntukkan RM2.11 bilion bagi tahun ini, peningkatan lebih RM500 juta berbanding 2025, selepas ia berbelanja melebihi peruntukan ditetapkan pada 2023, 2024 dan 2025.
Tetapi, katanya, peningkatan peruntukan itu masih tidak mencukupi, sekali gus mendorong Kementerian Kewangan mengambil langkah tambahan.

"Pertama, mengenal pasti penjimatan belanja pembangunan daripada kementerian lain dan setakat ini telah meluluskan perbelanjaan tambahan RM500 juta untuk 2026 dengan mengeluarkan surat kebenaran berbelanja melebihi peruntukan.
"Kedua, pada 10 Sept lalu, mengarahkan KKDW menangguh pengeluaran surat setuju terima baharu berhubung (projek) jalan luar bandar supaya tidak menambah lagi tunggakan bayaran (kepada kontraktor).

"Ketiga, memohon KKDW menyediakan unjuran keperluan peruntukan jalan luar bandar sehingga hujung 2026 dan 2027 berdasarkan kontrak yang telah dianugerahkan," katanya dalam jawapan bertulis di Parlimen.
Anwar yang juga perdana menteri menjawab soalan Lim Guan Eng (PH-Bagan) bagi memperincikan tindakan diambil terhadap pihak bertanggungjawab atas perbelanjaan berlebihan KKDW secara berterusan.
Lim turut bertanya sama ada kontraktor bagi projek KKDW dipilih melalui tender terbuka.

Anwar berkata, Perbendaharaan memperkenalkan sistem tender terbuka pra-kelayakan terpilih (TTPKT) di KKDW pada 2023, namun Laporan Ketua Audit Negara tahun lalu mendapati sistem baharu itu gagal mencapai objektif asal Putrajaya.
"Dengan itu, Kementerian Kewangan telah menghentikan kelulusan kaedah TTPKT oleh KKDW untuk projek baharu."
Bulan lalu, Zahid mendedahkan sebahagian kontraktor melaksanakan projek luar bandar lewat menerima bayaran daripada kerajaan sehingga ada yang terpaksa menutup operasi akibat masalah aliran tunai.

Susulan itu, Ketua Setiausaha Perbendaharaan, Johan Mahmood Merican dilaporkan berkata, sebahagian besar peruntukan tahun ini untuk projek jalan luar bandar sudah dibelanjakan menyebabkan kekangan pembayaran.

Katanya, peruntukan itu telah diagihkan sepenuhnya, manakala KKDW secara konsisten berbelanja melebihi peruntukan tahunan diluluskan untuk projek jalan luar bandar sejak beberapa tahun ini, dengan jumlah perbelanjaan berlebihan terkumpul sebanyak RM2.1 bilion direkodkan dari 2023 hingga 2025.

df463636d13f62de: A German court has issued an injunction banning SAP from providing certain features of its Signavio product, following a legal challenge from process mining biz Celonis. The ruling only applies to implementations in Germany, but is part of a broader legal tussle between the two companies over intellectual property. This case focuses on software which helps companies understand their own complex business processes in order to improve them and help prepare for an application migration. The Munich Regional Court ruled against SAP for infringing a Celonis patent covering the technology which determines the lead time between process stages of a process instance. The court also asked SAP to provide more information and offer financial statements about its alleged infringement. In a statement, an SAP spokesperson said: “The court’s ruling relates to one specific function within SAP Signavio Process Intelligence, not to the product as a whole. SAP Signavio Process Intelligence remains available to customers. S/4HANA Cloud migrations are not affected. SAP is working to ensure that there is no disruption to our customers.” SAP added: "SAP respectfully disagrees with the Munich court's ruling and has appealed the decision. SAP has separately challenged the validity of the asserted patent before the Federal Patent Court. In fact, the Munich court's decision represents only one of several ongoing disputes between SAP and Celonis, including patent actions brought by SAP in Germany and the United States. SAP’s first priority is ensuring that there is no disruption to our customers, and we will address all related matters through the appropriate legal channels." Celonis specializes in process mining, building software designed to gather data from people's interactions with business applications. It aims to uncover how organizations’ processes are actually performed, as opposed to how they were designed. For example, during a process mining project, pharma giant GSK discovered around 28,000 different variations for the process of running a sales order. Celonis was founded in 2011 and early customers included Siemens, with projects examining how processes run on the global engineering company’s SAP software. In 2021, SAP decided it wanted in on the same market and bought mining company Signavio, in part to help customers move from legacy software systems to the cloud. The ERP giant does not mandate Signavio for its migrations, but the software is bundled in packages under the moniker RISE with SAP, the lift-shift-and-transform commercial push SAP launched in 2021 to get users into the cloud and on its latest ERP offering, S/4HANA. The latest ruling is part of a set of legal disputes between Celonis and SAP. In March last year, Celonis filed a lawsuit in the US Court, Northern District of California, claiming the ERP giant had made it more difficult and expensive for third-party software companies to get hold of customer data stored in SAP's business software. Celonis was later allowed to amend and refile its complaint after the US court dismissed most of the claims. A trial is set for September 2027. SAP has also launched a case alleging a patent infringement action against Celonis at a Düsseldorf, Germany, court. It also filed suit in October last year at the District Court of Delaware over four US patents. Celonis has launched other cases alleging infringement by SAP, including in a Texas federal district court. ®

5e02b63d3dd139c5: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 19 — Stroke can happen at any age, including newborns and teenagers, and delays in recognising the symptoms can lead to lasting neurological and developmental complications.

Consultant Paediatrician and Paediatric Neurologist at Sunway Medical Centre Velocity (SMCV) Dr Tan Jen Ern said childhood stroke, although uncommon, could easily be overlooked because its symptoms often resemble other childhood illnesses.

“Paediatric stroke is rare, but rarity does not mean it cannot happen. The important message is to recognise sudden neurological changes and seek emergency assessment promptly,” he said in a statement today.

The Paediatric Protocols for Malaysian Hospitals, developed by the Health Ministry and the Malaysian Paediatric Association, estimate that childhood stroke affects between 2.5 and 13 cases per 100,000 children annually.
Dr Tan said children might not be able to describe their symptoms clearly, while a lack of awareness among parents and healthcare professionals could delay diagnosis and treatment.

“In older children and teenagers, stroke can look much like it does in adults with facial drooping, weakness on one side of the body or difficulty speaking, while babies and toddlers may show more subtle signs such as seizures or difficulty feeding,” he said.
Because stroke is rarely expected in children, parents may wait to see if symptoms pass. However, stroke remains a time-sensitive emergency regardless of age.

Dr Tan advised parents to note when their child was last known to be well and call an ambulance immediately if stroke was suspected, as the timing of symptom onset is important in determining emergency treatment options.

Calling an ambulance allows the emergency system to help coordinate the appropriate destination and facilitate transfer to a facility with stroke expertise. The nearest hospital is not always the one best equipped for an acute stroke.

“Time is brain. If the facility cannot promptly provide the necessary brain and vascular imaging or specialist assessment, the child may need to be referred or transferred, which can mean additional time before the diagnosis is confirmed and specialised treatment can be considered,” he said.

Dr Tan said childhood stroke could be associated with heart disease, abnormalities of the brain’s blood vessels, blood disorders, infections or inflammation, trauma and certain genetic or metabolic conditions, even in children who appeared healthy.

“In most cases, these children have an underlying condition that has yet to be identified. In my practice, the most common underlying cause is an abnormality of the brain’s blood vessels,” said Dr Tan.

He said investigations to determine the underlying cause could include blood tests, screening for blood-clotting disorders where needed, heart assessments, including an electrocardiogram (ECG) and an echocardiogram, and magnetic resonance imaging with angiography (MRI with MRA) to examine the brain and its blood vessels.

Initial treatment focuses on stabilising the child, controlling seizures and managing complications, with clot-preventing medications used depending on the cause. For selected children who meet strict criteria, a minimally invasive procedure to remove the clot from a blocked artery (endovascular thrombectomy) may be considered with the necessary expertise.

Beyond the immediate medical emergency, childhood stroke could affect attention, memory, learning, communication, emotional regulation and social participation, even when a child appeared to have recovered physically.

“A child may have a relatively good physical recovery but continue to experience difficulties with attention, processing speed, memory, learning, communication, emotional regulation, social participation or confidence, which can have a major effect on school, relationships and everyday life,” he said.
Dr Tan said long-term follow-up is important because some developmental and learning difficulties may only become apparent when children enter school and face greater academic and social demands.

He urged parents to seek immediate medical attention if their child suddenly developed weakness on one side, facial asymmetry, difficulty speaking or an unexplained seizure, stressing that care should focus not only on treating the stroke but also on supporting the child’s development and quality of life.
Meanwhile, SMCV will hold its neuroscience public event, “Brain for Life: The Ultimate Mind & Motion Experience”, from Oct 30 to Nov 1 at the Main Atrium, Ground Floor, Sunway Velocity Mall.
From stroke awareness to memory and brain health, the event covers neurological wellbeing across every stage of life.

Highlights include SunMed Kids’ Club FAST Heroes Campaign by the Angels Initiative (A workshop for children to learn and identify stroke symptoms), interactive game stations, a panel discussion on memory loss and early Alzheimer’s disease, complimentary consultations with SMCV’s neuroscience consultants, complimentary health assessments, and promotions on selected health screening packages.

Visitors can also experience Malaysia’s first educational Stroke Mirror. While not a diagnostic tool, it shows a simulated representation of stroke-related symptoms, helping families learn one of the most recognisable warning signs together. — Bernama
47e37c665a3c344b: HOUSTON, Oct 19 — One preaches love and reconciliation. The other champions confrontation and unyielding conservatism. Both invoke Christianity as they battle for a US Senate seat in Texas that could help determine control of Congress.

Democrat James Talarico, a 37-year-old former teacher and aspiring Presbyterian minister, faces Republican Ken Paxton, a 63-year-old political survivor whose loyalty to President Donald Trump has helped him overcome years of scandal.
Their contest on November 3 has become unexpectedly competitive in a state where no Democrat has won statewide office since 1994, presenting voters with two sharply contrasting political figures.
James Talarico: ‘Politics of love’
As a child at his church’s daycare centre, James Talarico would intervene to break up fights, according to the pastor who has known him since infancy.
Jim Rigby, who baptised Talarico and married his parents, remembers the youngster as a “calming presence.”
Decades later, that temperament has become central to the Democrat’s appeal.

A former middle school teacher and nonprofit director, Talarico was elected to the Texas House of Representatives in 2018 and has built a national following with speeches that fuse progressive politics, biblical teachings and criticism of America’s wealthy elites.
“I’ll always put Texas before any political party,” he has declared.
A Presbyterian seminarian, Talarico draws inspiration from Jesus’s commandment to love one’s neighbour, arguing that faith demands compassion for the poor, immigrants and marginalised communities.
He has challenged conservative Christians on their own theological ground, condemning Christian nationalism and opposing government-sponsored religious displays in public schools.
His political message combines support for abortion rights and greater economic equality with appeals to voters weary of partisan hostility.

Talarico’s conversational style and command of scripture have generated viral social media clips, while a two-hour appearance on comedian Joe Rogan’s hugely popular podcast in 2025 introduced him to an audience beyond traditional Democratic circles.
But his progressive theology has provoked fierce criticism from religious conservatives, particularly over his positions on abortion and LGBTQ rights.
His suggestion that God is “nonbinary” drew accusations of blasphemy, while his more cautious recent language on transgender issues has raised questions among some of his own supporters.
Talarico has sought to broaden his appeal by defending Texas’s oil industry and criticising aspects of former president Joe Biden’s immigration policies.
He defeated the more combative congresswoman Jasmine Crockett in the Democratic primary, promising a “politics of love.”
Ken Paxton: The MAGA survivor
Ken Paxton’s political career has repeatedly appeared close to collapse.

Yet the Texas attorney general has survived criminal charges, impeachment and years of damaging revelations to emerge as one of the most recognisable champions of Trump’s Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement.
A lawyer educated at Baylor University and the University of Virginia, Paxton entered the Texas legislature in 2003 and made his name challenging the Republican establishment from the right.
He became attorney general in 2015, turning the office into a formidable legal weapon against Democratic administrations and progressive causes.
His lawsuits targeting immigration policies, abortion access, environmental regulations and the Biden administration made him a hero to grassroots conservatives.
Paxton also supported Trump’s attempts to overturn his 2020 election defeat, cementing his standing with the president’s most loyal supporters.

Like Talarico, Paxton places religion at the centre of his politics, but he champions a different vision of Christianity, one that emphasises traditional morality and the defence of a nation he believes was founded on biblical principles.
“In Texas classrooms, we want the Word of God opened, the Ten Commandments displayed and prayers lifted up,” he declared in 2025.
His political resilience has nevertheless been tested by repeated scandals.
In 2023, the Republican-controlled Texas House impeached him over allegations of corruption and abuse of power, but the state Senate acquitted him.
Long-running securities fraud charges were also resolved without an admission of wrongdoing under an agreement requiring restitution and community service.
More recently, his marriage collapsed amid allegations of infidelity, while fresh reporting has raised questions about his relationships with wealthy donors and businessmen.
Paxton denies wrongdoing and has portrayed his legal and political troubles as efforts by establishment figures to destroy him.
His supporters have largely stood by him, valuing his willingness to fight their political battles over questions about his personal conduct.
That loyalty helped him defeat four-term incumbent senator John Cornyn by 28 percentage points in a Republican primary runoff in May after Trump threw his weight behind Paxton.
It was a striking demonstration of how thoroughly Trump’s movement has reshaped Texas Republican politics. — AFP
4f78f21c32ddc814: BETHLEHEM, Oct 19 — In a US city once known for its steel industry, workers enjoy family outings beside retired, rust-streaked blast furnaces.
This massive steel mill in Bethlehem, Pennsylvania, fell silent in the 1990s.
But the partially redeveloped industrial site came alive again at a recent Oktoberfest event featuring attendees in Bavarian dress, large beer steins and a massive screen playing American football.
Among the event’s attendees were supporters of President Donald Trump, who stand by his Republican Party, despite disappointments.
Commercial roofer Nev Hamm recalled living “right behind” the steel plant in the 1980s, when it was still running.
“It was good and they screwed up here. They gave it away,” the 62-year-old told AFP.
But he believes that industry is “coming back” thanks to Trump’s protectionist policies.
“It’s gonna be better as soon as we’re done with the Iranian war,” Hamm added, referring to the US-Israel war with Iran that started in late February.
Bethlehem sits at the heart of the Lehigh Valley, a former US stronghold of heavy industry.
Workers now find jobs in logistics, food manufacturing — especially pet food — and a growing pharmaceutical sector, with a plant for weight-loss drugs opening soon.
Beth Piniella, 40, feels that her family is doing all right.
“I make decent money,” she told AFP of her job cleaning a warehouse for a packaging and business supplies distributor.
On Trump, for whom she voted, she added: “I really think it’s hit or miss on certain things.”
Nearby, her husband Brian said he was “a little disappointed.”
“I thought prices were coming down,” he said.
‘Stuck’

A person walks past the former Bethlehem Steel plant, now part of the SteelStacks arts and entertainment campus, in Bethlehem, Pennsylvania, on October 4, 2026. — AFP pic
The district where they live could tip control of the US House of Representatives to Democrats following the November 3 midterm elections.
Republican incumbent Ryan Mackenzie won by a narrow margin in 2024.
His Democratic rival is Bob Brooks, a former firefighter and political newcomer who positions himself as a voice for the working class.
Still, voters like Henry Martin plan to skip the polls entirely this time, frustrated with both major political parties.
“They’re living the high life,” said the 32-year-old warehouse manager. “The everyday average Joe like me, we’re not doing great at all.”
He feels “stuck” between the “terrible” rent he has to pay and home prices that are “insanely out of reach.”
In nearby Allentown, a billboard urges drivers to vote for Brooks.
Ramona Chery, who works at a tire shop just below the sign, said the city’s large Latino community has been shaken by Trump’s hardline immigration policies and inflation.
Gains among Latino voters in the 2024 presidential election helped return Trump to the White House.
But Chery said: “There’s more poverty than before.”
‘Enough is enough’

Construction workers at a job site in downtown Allentown, Pennsylvania, on October 6, 2026. Mike Shupp, who is president of the local United Auto Workers’ union, said: “I wish there was a manufacturing boom, but I’m not seeing it.”
At his office in Allentown, the labor leader recounted how the area used to be lined with manufacturing facilities.
He worries that American truck manufacturer Mack will continue cutting US production, shifting jobs to Mexico.
About a 20-minute drive away, the region’s last remaining Mack plant employs some 2,800 people.
The company had announced plans to lay off up to 350 workers at the facility in April 2025, partly due to Trump’s tariffs.
Around 170 employees were ultimately let go, only to be recalled when business conditions improved — and Trump himself visited the site in June to tout his policies.
“I wasn’t interested in being involved with that,” said Shawn Smith, 52, a technician who puts finishing touches on heavy trucks.
Smith, a union representative, supports Democratic candidate Brooks.
He added that workers “don’t talk politics” at the plant as it “just starts an argument.”
Nonetheless, he believes: “There’s enough of a disconnect, and there’s enough independents and Republicans that (will) say enough is enough, and they want a little bit of a change.” — AFP
bacd267802ec61e8: PHILADELPHIA, Oct 19 — LeBron James, yearning to capture a fifth career NBA title, tips off his record 24th campaign tomorrow at age 41 with his new Philadelphia 76ers teammates chasing a long-sought crown.
The league’s 81st season launches with the Sixers at New York, watching the Knicks hoist their first championship banner since 1973.
James made it clear in July when he announced he was joining the 76ers that his move was all about making one more title run himself.
“I believe I can help make the Philadelphia 76ers a championship team and I am so excited to energise a new fan base and start this incredible journey one last time,” James posted on X on July 24.

“I’m not going for money. I’m not going for family. What am I really playing for at this point? I still want to sacrifice. I still want to work. I still want to grind. I still want to compete, to win and to have a chance at the feeling of winning another championship.”

James, the NBA’s all-time leading scorer, said in June he was leaving the Los Angeles Lakers. On July 24, James revealed he was going to Philadelphia and two days later, the team revealed James had signed a two-year deal worth $8 million.

James, a four-time NBA Most Valuable Player, won two NBA titles with Miami, another with hometown club Cleveland and a fourth with the Lakers and hopes to bring the 76ers their first NBA title since 1983.
He could become the first player to win NBA titles with four or more clubs.
It’s a goal that James, who turns 42 in December, shares with former Boston star Jaylen Brown, Joel Embiid, Tyrese Maxey and VJ Edgecombe — all seeking a first NBA title.
“Everybody is kind of on the same page,” James said. “We want to put the work in. That’s most important.
“Everyone is highly motivated to get 1 per cent better every single day... Everyone is excited to be here and that’s exciting to be a part of.
“If we’re trying to do something special, which I believe we are, it’s a positive. If you have this championship approach every day, it’ll definitely work in our favor.”
James has career averages of 26.8 points, 7.5 rebounds, 7.4 assists and 1.5 steals over 1,622 games.
James said his teammates are willing to make sacrfices to become a contender, not content with big individual statistics and early playoff exits.
“I don’t think anybody in the locker room wants their career to be like that or we wouldn’t be here,” James said.
James hopes to help 2024 US Olympic gold medal teammate Embiid grab his first NBA crown.
“Hopefully I can give him resources and whatever he needs on a day-to-day basis to make him feel even more comfortable about where he is, about where we are as a team,” James said.
James had 10 points, five assists and four rebounds in his pre-season debut for the 76ers in a 114-108 loss at Brooklyn.
“It felt a little different,” James said. “Obviously, just wearing a new uniform, but the game is the game.
“We’re still trying to put each other in a position to be successful and complement each other the best way we can out on the floor. But it’s going to take some time.”
No ‘instant oatmeal’
James said people who want quick and easy camaraderie will be disappointed.

“They want instant oatmeal,” James said. “If you want to do something special, it takes time, every single day doing things you may not want to do, because it’s the same thing over and over and over and over.
“For us to be great we have to do things that are just not comfortable. We have to be comfortable being uncomfortable. That’s the best way to expedite being great.
“I didn’t leave my family to lose in the second round I know that for sure. Work needs to be done and I’m ready to put the work in.” — AFP
5e32330c30acb1b5: LOS ANGELES, Oct 19 — Jalen Brunson and the New York Knicks say they’re starting from scratch as they aim for an elusive NBA championship repeat with the San Antonio Spurs spearheading a host of rivals as the 2026 season tips off tomorrow.

“We just have to find a way to turn the page and move on,” NBA Finals Most Valuable Player Brunson said as the Knicks began their preparations in September three months after ending the storied franchise’s 53-year title drought with an epic defeat of San Antonio.

The Knicks return their starting five, but a sour note has already been sounded in the pre-season as star centre Karl-Anthony Towns said he was “extremely disappointed” by the Knicks’ public announcement that they were pausing contract extension talks with him and Josh Hart.
Additionally, no team has won back-to-back titles since the Golden State Warriors in 2018, and Victor Wembanyama’s Spurs are just one of the clubs tipped to keep it that way.
The Oklahoma City Thunder, led by two-time reigning MVP Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, are eager to reassert themselves after the Spurs ended their title repeat bid in the Western Conference finals.

Closer to home in the Eastern Conference the Knicks will contend with a retooled Philadelphia 76ers squad now featuring all-time leading scorer LeBron James and Jaylen Brown, who earned Finals MVP honours with the Boston Celtics in 2024.
Four-time champion James, still a force at 41, agreed to slash his salary in his quest for a fifth ring.
Along with Brown he’ll team with former MVP big man Joel Embiid, All-NBA point guard Tyrese Maxey and 21-year-old phenom VJ Edgecombe.
The 76ers will be out to make an early statement when they take on the Knicks at Madison Square Garden tomorrow, part of a three-game opening day slate.

The Miami Heat have also added star power in the shape of two-time MVP Giannis Antetokounmpo. Antetokounmpo, who led Milwaukee to the crown in 2021, arrived from the Bucks in a blockbuster trade and could form a lethal partnership with Bam Adebayo — who poured in 83 points in one game last season.
But nowhere are the expectations higher than in San Antonio. The Knicks were still celebrating their Finals victory when Wembanyama started counting the days to the 2027 championship series.
San Antonio used the disappointment of their 2013 Finals loss to Miami to fuel their run to the 2014 title, and Wembanyama says the current Spurs squad is determined to bounce back in the same way.
Spurs eye summit
“We’re fighting for the top spot of the mountain,” says the towering French centre, who reached his first NBA Finals in only his third season.

At just 22 Wembanyama is a bona fide star. He was the 2026 Defensive Player of the Year and finished third in MVP voting. An abundance of other talented players at coach Mitch Johnson’s disposal includes Dylan Harper, who emerged as a consistent threat at the rim in the playoffs after being limited by injuries in the regular season.
The annual pre-season survey of league general managers saw the Spurs tipped to take it all.
Gilgeous-Alexander and the Thunder expect to have something to say about that.
Oklahoma City took the Spurs to seven games in last season’s Western Conference finals despite the injury struggles of key offensive contributors Jalen Williams and Ajay Mitchell during the series.

With Williams and Mitchell healthy the Thunder are poised to maintain their offensive efficiency while All-Star big man Chet Holmgren and Isaiah Hartenstein return to anchor the league’s best defence.

The Minnesota Timberwolves, who reached the Western Conference finals in 2024 and 2025, are counting on the arrival of LaMelo Ball to team with Anthony Edwards to ramp up their challenge to the Spurs and Thunder.
In Los Angeles, Slovenian star Luka Doncic and Austin Reaves spearhead the new-look Lakers, aiming to forge a new identity after the departure of James in free agency. — AFP
c0d505ca59a4244c: LISBON, Oct 19 — Juan Mayorga smiled as a stingray glided across his computer screen, moving gracefully over the seabed near Portugal’s Desertas Islands, part of the Madeira archipelago in the Atlantic Ocean.
“It’s a good day when we see animals like this,” said the Colombian environmental engineer, who is analysing underwater footage to measure the effects of marine protection.
“This is conservation in action,” said Mayorga, 36, who works for Pristine Seas, a marine conservation initiative run by the National Geographic Society.
“As we protect the place, year after year, fish get bigger and bigger and bigger, produce more and more babies, and that is protection working right there.”
Mayorga is among nearly 200 scientists taking part in a month-long expedition in October to study the marine environment around Madeira, the birthplace of football superstar Cristiano Ronaldo.

Juan Mayorga, marine scientist with National Geographic Pristine Seas, points to a laptop screen displaying BRUVS underwater footage while reviewing collected data with Emanuel Gonçalves, chief scientist and board member of the Oceano Azul Foundation, inside the ship off the coast of Madeira on October 12, 2026 during the ‘Madeira Ocean’ scientific expedition. — AFP pic
Researchers aboard around 15 vessels are investigating the archipelago’s marine life, assessing the health of its ecosystems and exploring how they can better withstand climate change.
Mayorga is analysing underwater video recorded at depths of 40 to 50 metres (130 to 165 feet) by cameras mounted on metal frames baited to attract fish.
He is particularly interested in comparing waters south of the Desertas Islands, where fishing is completely prohibited, with those to the north, where some fishing is still allowed.
The comparison offers a glimpse of how different levels of protection affect marine life.
‘Real fight’
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
A diver wearing a yellow tank and yellow fins swims above a rocky seabed off the coast of Madeira on October 11, 2026 during the ‘Madeira Ocean’ scientific expedition. — AFP pic

The expedition’s flagship is the 70-metre sailing ship Santa Maria Manuela, which has brought researchers to the Desertas Islands, a group of three uninhabited rocky islets about 40 kilometres (25 miles) south-east of Madeira.
Rising steeply from the Atlantic, the islands’ rust-coloured cliffs, rocky slopes and windswept ridges form a protected nature reserve where seabirds circle above the waves.
On the largest island, Rui Seabra, a 44-year-old researcher from the University of Porto, attaches temperature sensors to rocks exposed at low tide along a small cove.
He wants to understand how crustaceans and sponges fare in sunny and shaded areas, information that could help scientists predict how marine biodiversity will respond to rising temperatures.

“We need to understand how biodiversity will be redistributed, which species will migrate where, what the conditions are here, how they will change, and which species we expect to find here in the future,” he said.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

A researcher wearing blue gloves uses tweezers to pick up a biological specimen from a tray aboard the ship off the coast of Madeira on October 11, 2026 during the ‘Madeira Ocean’ scientific expedition. — AFP pic
Nearby, a marine biologist aboard an inflatable boat collected environmental DNA samples from the water.
The technique can reveal which fish species are present even when they evade the cameras.
“We are on the front lines of the real fight to find solutions that allow us to address problems on the ground,” said expedition leader Emanuel Goncalves.
‘Best weapon’
The fieldwork comes as a UN biodiversity summit, known as COP17, gets underway Monday in Armenia to discuss efforts to protect the world’s natural ecosystems.
Goncalves, chief scientist at Portugal’s Oceano Azul Foundation, a marine conservation non-profit, acknowledges the importance of international meetings in setting political priorities.
But “the urgency to act does not allow us to wait for decisions that sometimes take decades,” he said.
Madeira has long been a pioneer in marine conservation.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

(From left) Marine biologists Gustavo Sousa, David Jacinto, David Milla Figueras, and Eva Iniguez, dive safety officer Cristiano Samagaio, and research technician Laura Piazzese prepare for a dive aboard an inflatable motorboat off the coast of Madeira on October 11, 2026, during the ‘Madeira Ocean’ scientific expedition. — AFP pic

The archipelago includes the main island of Madeira, the beach destination of Porto Santo, the Desertas Islands and the remote Selvagens Islands, about 280 kilometres farther south toward Spain’s Canary Islands.
In 1971, authorities established a reserve around the Selvagens Islands to protect Cory’s shearwaters, seabirds found around Madeira and other Atlantic islands.
Expanded in 2022, the reserve now covers about 2,600 square kilometres (1,000 square miles), making it the largest protected marine area in the North Atlantic.

Another reserve established around the Desertas Islands in the early 1990s has helped a colony of Mediterranean monk seals, one of Europe’s most endangered marine mammals, grow from just eight animals to 31.
“An ocean in a good state of conservation is the best weapon we have against climate change,” said Paulo Oliveira, coordinator of the Madeira Ocean conservation programme launched in May. — AFP

178da8d59451097a: Microsoft has acknowledged that the October 2026 Windows Server updates may be destabilizing Exchange Server. The problems are related to this list of Windows Server updates (see here) and Microsoft makes it clear they are not related to the October 2026 security updates for Exchange Server. The software giant says the bug can hit Exchange Servers running Windows Server 2016, 2019, 2022, and 2025. The glitch might not be immediate and could impact Exchange Server OWA, which can throw up connection glitches or cause lengthy email queues, "with email crawling to a halt." Rebooting the server might make the problem go away temporarily, but a more permanent workaround is a registry edit. The destabilization issue could impact Exchange Server 2016, 2019, and the new Subscription Edition (SE), says the Windows maker. Microsoft strongly advised that customers should not uninstall the October 2026 Windows Server update and stated, "Not all Exchange servers will be impacted by installation of those updates equally; the severity and speed of impact varies based on Exchange server load. Some servers might never see a problem." However, for those administrators who found their weekend swallowed by borked Exchange Servers, the registry edit is currently the only workaround. The cause of the issue is a default limit on the amount of memory used by Endpoint Mapper when handling Endpoint Lookup calls. In Microsoft's Release Health Dashboard for Windows Server 2025 (Server 2022, 2019, and 2016 are also affected), the Microsoft said: "For workloads such as Exchange Server, the default limit of 512 simultaneous Endpoint Lookup calls might not be sufficient under heavy load." Hence, the instruction to use a registry setting to increase the maximum. It added, "We are investigating this issue and will provide more information when it is available." Customers were understandably frustrated. On Microsoft's support page, one wrote, "We have had the problem like every 20h since Wednesday, when we installed the windows updates for October and the exchange su. Reboot only solution," before noting that the registry setting appeared to have improved things. Another fumed, "Also please release your updates tested and without problems. Without giving us the job to test for you. We're already paying for the software and you want to make tests with us?! I spent all weekend on my servers because of this." The issue is bad form on the part of Microsoft and appears to be the result of a poorly thought-through default applied in the operating system which impacted Exchange Server. Microsoft has yet to commit to issuing an out-of-band update to resolve the issue, after all, not every customer is affected, and the problem depends heavily on how busy a server is. However, at least there's a registry workaround that might do the trick while Microsoft ponders its next move. ®

6e3c2a3abbd41e1a: Microsoft has reportedly pulled out of plans for Britain's largest AI supercomputer, because the government-backed project is facing the rather inconvenient problem of having no electricity to run it. The tech giant has terminated its agreement with British AI infrastructure startup Nscale for a planned datacenter in Loughton, Essex, according to The Telegraph, which first reported the withdrawal on Sunday. The decision follows reports that the site, which was supposed to begin operating in 2027, might not receive enough electricity from the grid until the early to mid-2030s. Microsoft was expected to be the anchor customer at Loughton, which Nscale had pitched as the UK's largest sovereign AI datacenter. Its departure leaves Nscale without a publicly announced customer for the site, although the neocloud insists the project is still going ahead. When the deal was announced in September 2025, the plan was to pack 23,040 Nvidia GB300 GPUs into a 50MW facility, with room to expand to 90MW. Microsoft would use the computing power for its Azure cloud services, with the first chips expected in early 2027. One important detail remained: how to power it. As The Guardian reported last month, UK Power Networks warned Nscale that the grid capacity needed might not be available until the 2030s. A UK Power Networks spokesperson told The Register it could not discuss individual connections due to obligations under Section 105 of the Utilities Act. "However, in general, many datacenters, whilst they can connect to our distribution network, are awaiting works on the national transmission network which we do not own," the spokesperson said. Nscale, meanwhile, isn't letting the small matter of losing its biggest customer dampen its enthusiasm. “We remain committed to both the Loughton project and the UK and we are exploring alternative power sources for the site, in addition to other expansion sites in the UK. Our relationship with Microsoft remains strong and long-term, and this unfortunate London-wide grid issue has no impact on our other contracts,” Nscale told The Register. Microsoft did not respond to a request for comment. The project has already had its share of awkward moments. In March, it was revealed that the site earmarked for Britain's AI supercomputer was still being used as a scaffolding yard. Nscale has since cleared the land, but removing the scaffolding has proved easier than securing electricity. The government might be feeling a little red-faced too, having trumpeted the Loughton project as part of Microsoft's £22 billion UK investment announcement in September 2025. Just over a year later, Microsoft has walked away, and the site is still facing years of delays in getting the power it needs. The grid problems extend well beyond Essex. Ofgem proposed charging datacenter developers for connection requests earlier this year, hoping to discourage speculative projects from clogging up the queue. Demand for new connections had surged from 41GW to 125GW in less than a year, with datacenters accounting for at least 80GW. Some UK datacenter developers have turned to gas-powered generation rather than wait years for a grid connection, while others face growing resistance from the people living nearby. Residents near Google's Waltham Cross facility complained about noise, lighting and poor consultation at a public meeting in July. Britain isn’t alone in finding that the AI boom comes with substantial infrastructure demands. In the US, public enthusiasm for datacenters appears to be cooling, with concerns about electricity costs and environmental impacts increasingly souring attitudes towards new developments. For all the billions being thrown at AI infrastructure, the industry is discovering that building datacenters is the easy part. Getting them connected to the grid, and keeping the neighbors happy, is proving rather more difficult. ®

In line with this, KWAP continues to explore investment opportunities through Dana Pemacu, an initiative supporting the Government-Linked Enterprises Activation and Reform Programme (GEAR-uP) under the Ekonomi MADANI framework.
Among its identified target sectors are the silver economy and healthcare, including products and services catering to the needs of older people.
Jay Khairil said preparing for an ageing society also requires improving access to services for retirees, including through digital platforms and community-based assistance.
He said KWAP was working to improve its MyPesara platforms and provide assistance to retirees in their communities.

“Technology has made many services more convenient. But we must ensure that it does not create a new divide. Some retirees are confident navigating an app; others are more comfortable speaking to someone directly. Both deserve services that work for them,” he said.

He also highlighted KWAP’s collaboration with the Malaysian Research Institute on Ageing (MyAgeing) at Universiti Putra Malaysia (UPM), which began in 2017 and led to the development of the Retirement Strategic Agenda in 2024.

The three-day NCA 2026 is jointly organised by MyAgeing, UPM, Kendana Malaysia, KWAP and the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), focusing on addressing inequalities and improving health, social support and technological solutions for older people. — Bernama
0950dcc29261b1f3: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 19 — The mechanism for allocating parliamentary constituency funds and the influx of foreign nationals were among the issues raised during the policy-stage debate on the Supply Bill today.

Syahredzan Johan (PH-Bangi) urged the government to enact legislation to ensure constituency allocations for MPs were distributed according to a proportional formula based on the number of voters and residents, regardless of political affiliation.

“If Bangi receives the same allocation as other constituencies with far fewer voters, it would create an injustice, as voters in Bangi would have to accept, based on a rough calculation, an allocation per voter that is lower than in other areas,” he said.

“We want to know the progress of projects, whether they are delayed, facing problems or cancelled, and who has been awarded the projects. Datuk Dr Radzi Jidin (PN-Putrajaya) urged the government to tighten national border security controls and conduct integrated operations to comprehensively curb the entry of undocumented migrants. Interjecting during the debate speech by Datuk Wan Saifulruddin Wan Jan (PN-Tasek Gelugor), he said the measure was important as Malaysia prepared to enter an ageing society phase, given that many people, particularly Malays, preferred to care for their parents at home rather than place them in care centres.

He also urged the Health Ministry, the Women, Family and Community Development Ministry, Economy Ministry and the Finance Ministry to conduct a financing-mapping study to coordinate welfare funding for senior citizens in a holistic manner.

71c6a43f3ae4c76f: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 19 — Malaysian entrepreneurs must overcome an inherent tendency toward excessive humility and actively build strong storytelling capabilities if they want to secure international venture capital, said Finance Minister II Datuk Seri Amir Hamzah Azizan.

a677158da1cd8619: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 19 — Seputeh MP Teresa Kok has won RM250,000 in damages in her defamation suit against Umno Youth chief Datuk Dr Muhamad Akmal Saleh over remarks he made during a dispute on halal certification.

f6400553710f72d1: A 16-year-old security flaw in Broadcom's Wi-Fi software could let attackers hijack millions of routers without knowing the network password, even though the chipmaker reportedly knew about the problem since 2018. Security researcher Quentin Kaiser disclosed the vulnerability, dubbed "WPSplinter," revealing two bugs in Broadcom's proprietary Wi-Fi implementation that date back to at least 2010. An attempted fix arrived eight years later, but Kaiser claims it didn't fully resolve the problem. The bugs lie in Broadcom's handling of Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS), the feature that lets users connect devices to a wireless network without manually entering a password. Kaiser found that specially crafted WPS messages could corrupt the router's memory, allowing someone within Wi-Fi range to run their own code on the device. They wouldn't need the Wi-Fi password, and the router's owner wouldn't have to do a thing. Kaiser demonstrated working exploits against routers supplied by Belgian internet providers Proximus and Orange. In one attack against an ASKEY TCG3000 gateway, he ran code on the device, pulled its Wi-Fi password from memory, and sent it back over the air. He then used the stolen credentials to join the network. He also found the flaw in Netgear and Technicolor routers supplied by VOO. He estimates that around 850,000 Proximus gateways could be affected, along with 500,000 at VOO and 210,000 at Orange Belgium. That puts the potential total at 1.56 million routers in Belgium alone, although Kaiser admits the figures are rough estimates. However, the problem is unlikely to stop at the Belgian border. Broadcom's Wi-Fi technology is used by dozens of manufacturers across hundreds of products, meaning the number of affected devices worldwide could be considerably higher. According to Kaiser, the chipmaker knew about the vulnerability back in 2018 and released a partial fix without publicly disclosing the problem. It subsequently recommended that manufacturers move away from its proprietary implementation and use the open-source hostapd software instead. Owners of routers running Broadcom's older eCos-based chips, including the BCM3380, BCM3383, and BCM33834, are in a particularly grim position. Kaiser calls the flaw a "forever day," meaning those devices may never get a fix. Routers using Linux-based BCM3390, BCM65xx, and BCM68xx chips aren't necessarily off the hook either, unless their manufacturers switch to hostapd. That leaves some older routers with no obvious route to a fix, while others depend on their manufacturers updating software that may be years out of support. Kaiser first reported the vulnerabilities to Broadcom on July 18, followed by a second report on July 27, giving the company and affected vendors 90 days before public disclosure. Broadcom responded on July 28 to say a patch was available and advised him to contact affected manufacturers directly. The following day, however, the company declined to assign a CVE identifier or provide him with a copy of the notification it said it had sent to manufacturers through its customer portal. Kaiser also contacted Proximus, attempted to reach Orange Belgium and VOO, and passed his findings to Belgium's national cybersecurity authorities. He subsequently opened a case with CERT/CC, which closed it on August 4 because Broadcom was itself a CVE Numbering Authority and had declined to register the vulnerability. By October 15, a day before his presentation, Kaiser said none of the affected devices he had identified had received a patch. Kaiser hasn't reported evidence of attacks in the wild, but the potential for mischief is considerable. Someone parked outside a home or office could potentially compromise a vulnerable router, steal network credentials, or use their access to interfere with traffic. Kaiser also credited AI with speeding up the investigation. He reckons the work would ordinarily have taken him months, but with the help of frontier models, he finished it in less than a week. ®

ef358924a095ce93: Nearly 100 years after the dirigible Graf Zeppelin made the first nonstop airship journey across the Pacific Ocean, another airship has successfully completed a round-trip flight from New Mexico to Japan and back. But the significance of this modern feat was less about the journey's length and more about its purpose: demonstrating how a lighter-than-air platform can act as a cell phone tower in the sky.

The trans-Pacific flight that took place over a month between August and September 2026 was the most notable milestone yet for Sceye, a US aerospace company based near Albuquerque, New Mexico. Sceye has developed an uncrewed platform filled with helium for buoyancy and equipped with an electric-powered propeller for active propulsion, allowing it to resist most strong winds and keep hovering over the same location for long periods. The platform also uses top-mounted solar panels and onboard batteries to stay powered for stratospheric operations around the clock.

“We can stay over an area of operation, and we do that in the stratosphere right around 60,000 feet, so we're twice as high as air traffic and we're above the jet stream, and yet 30 times closer than low-Earth orbit satellites,” Mikkel Frandsen, founder and CEO of Sceye, told Ars. “We can fly through day and night until the sun comes up the next morning and recharges the batteries, at which point we're still at the same altitude and still over the same area of operation.”
